title: Why Patroni failover takes 26–49 seconds with default settings (and how to make it faster)
summary:
You build a Patroni + etcd + HAProxy cluster, kill the primary in a test, and your write loop stops for half a minute or more. Nothing is broken. That is what the default settings are designed to do. This post explains where those seconds go and what you can change.

The three settings that matter

All three live in Patroni's dynamic configuration (stored in the DCS, changed with patronictl edit-config). From the official documentation:

Setting What it is Default Minimum
loop_wait "the number of seconds the loop will sleep" between HA cycles 10 1
ttl the TTL of the leader lock; "think of it as the length of time before initiation of the automatic failover process" 30 20
retry_timeout "timeout for DCS and PostgreSQL operation retries"; "DCS or network issues shorter than this will not cause Patroni to demote the leader" 10 3

The documentation also sets a hard rule when you change them:

loop_wait + 2 * retry_timeout <= ttl

With defaults: 10 + 2 × 10 = 30 ≤ 30. The defaults sit exactly on the limit.

What happens when the primary dies

  1. While healthy, the primary renews the leader key in etcd on every HA loop, roughly every loop_wait (10 s).
  2. The primary crashes (power loss, kernel panic, hard network isolation). Nobody renews the key.
  3. The key lives until ttl (30 s) after its last renewal. Since renewals happen every ~10 s, the failure can land anywhere in that cycle: the key expires between ~20 s and ~30 s after the failure.
  4. A replica notices the key is gone on its next HA cycle (between 0 and loop_wait seconds later), checks it is healthy enough (for example within maximum_lag_on_failover), takes the key and promotes PostgreSQL.
  5. HAProxy, which polls each node's GET /primary (HTTP 200 only on the node "running as the primary with leader lock"), needs one or more successful checks on the new primary before it routes writes there. With checks every 2 s and a rise greater than 1, that adds a few more seconds.

Add up the pieces: 20–30 s for the key to expire, 0–10 s for a replica to notice, a second or two to promote, and a few seconds of health checks. You get the 26–49 s range you see with plain Patroni + etcd defaults and HAProxy checking every 2 s. The exact figure depends on where in the renewal cycle the failure happens, on how fast promotion completes, and on your health check settings.

Two important exceptions

  • Clean shutdown is fast. If you stop Patroni normally (systemctl stop patroni, a planned reboot) it releases the leader key on the way out, so a replica can take over without waiting for the TTL. That is why "I rebooted the primary and failover took 5 seconds" and "I pulled the power cable and it took 40" are both true.
  • A frozen primary is the slow case. A node that hangs (stuck I/O, process stopped) may keep its key until it expires, and it is still in HAProxy's backend until checks fail. This is the scenario to test, because it is the one that hurts most.

How to make it faster

1. Shrink ttl, loop_wait and retry_timeout together

For example:

# patronictl -c /etc/patroni/patroni.yml edit-config
loop_wait: 5
retry_timeout: 5
ttl: 20

5 + 2 × 5 = 15 ≤ 20, so the rule holds, and the worst-case key expiry drops from ~30 s to ~20 s after the last renewal. ttl cannot go below 20.

The trade-off is real:

  • A shorter retry_timeout means a shorter etcd or network hiccup is enough to demote a healthy primary. If your etcd runs on slow disks or across a flaky link, you will trade slow failovers for unnecessary ones.
  • A shorter loop_wait means more frequent DCS writes and more work per node.

Measure your etcd latency (etcdctl check perf, fsync metrics) before going aggressive.

2. Tune the HAProxy health checks

The usual Patroni HAProxy backend looks like this:

backend primary
    option httpchk GET /primary
    http-check expect status 200
    default-server inter 2s fall 3 rise 2 on-marked-down shutdown-sessions
    server db1 10.0.0.11:5432 check port 8008
    server db2 10.0.0.12:5432 check port 8008

inter × rise is the minimum time before the new primary receives traffic, and inter × fall the time before the old one is taken out. on-marked-down shutdown-sessions closes existing connections to a node marked down, so clients do not keep writing into a dead socket. Lowering inter to 1 s is cheap; it only adds HTTP requests to the Patroni REST API.

3. Make clients reconnect quickly

Database failover time is not application recovery time. Check your driver's connect timeout, TCP keepalives and retry logic. A pool that waits 2 minutes on a half-open TCP connection will hide every second you saved in Patroni.

4. Handle the frozen primary explicitly

Lower TTLs help, but a hung node is a detection problem, not just a timer problem. Options include Patroni's watchdog support (so a node that stops running its HA loop is reset) and external fencing that removes the old primary from every load balancer as soon as a failover is decided.

5. Measure, do not assume

Run a write loop through the load balancer and look at the gap:

while true; do
  psql -h VIRTUAL_IP -p 5000 -U app -d app -qAt \
    -c "INSERT INTO ha_test DEFAULT VALUES RETURNING now()" 2>&1
  sleep 0.5
done

Then try a switchover, a clean stop, a kill -9, and a SIGSTOP of Patroni and PostgreSQL on the primary (test environments only). Each one exercises a different path.

Summary

  • With defaults, the leader key expires 20–30 s after a hard failure; add detection, promotion and health checks and you land in 26–49 s.
  • Any change must respect loop_wait + 2 * retry_timeout <= ttl, and ttl cannot go below 20.
  • Faster settings increase the risk of demoting a healthy primary on short DCS hiccups.
  • HAProxy check intervals and client reconnect behaviour matter as much as Patroni's timers.

Disclosure: I work on HighAvailabilityData, a free on-premise console from NUTRADELIS S.L. for Patroni clusters. Instead of only waiting for the TTL, it lets the HAProxy instances and the console vote: if a strict majority sees the primary down for lb_failover_after (10 s by default), it promotes the healthy replica with the most WAL applied through Patroni's POST /failover, releases the stale leader key with a compare-and-delete and puts the old primary in maintenance on every HAProxy. In our tests writes came back in about 15–20 s; measure in your own environment. The original article includes a step-by-step test plan.

  • Patroni, REST API (GET /primary, POST /failover): https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/rest_api.html
  • Patroni, DCS Failsafe Mode (primary demoted when the leader lock update fails): https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/dcs_failsafe_mode.html
  • Patroni, Watchdog support: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/watchdog.html
  • HAProxy configuration manual (inter, fall, rise, on-marked-down): https://docs.haproxy.org/
  • Pigsty documentation, Patroni passive failure RTO model (best/worst case per phase): https://pigsty.io/docs/concept/ha/failure/passive/
  • HighAvailabilityData, original article: https://www.highavailabilitydata.com/resources/failover-postgresql?lang=en

                    ▼                                       ▼
     ┌─────────────────────────────┐         ┌─────────────────────────────┐
     │  ECS Fargate Task (Subnet A)│         │  ECS Fargate Task (Subnet B)│
     │  FastAPI + Docker (Port 8000)│        │  FastAPI + Docker (Port 8000)│
     │  Target Type: IP (awsvpc)   │         │  Target Type: IP (awsvpc)   │
     └──────────────┬──────────────┘         └──────────────┬──────────────┘
                    │                                       │
        ┌───────────┴───────────┬───────────────────────────┴───────────┐
        ▼                       ▼                                       ▼
┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────────────┐               ┌──────────────────────┐
│  Amazon ECR  │     │ CloudWatch Log Group │               │ External Database    │
│  Repository  │     │  (/ecs/fastapi-ecs)  │               │ (Supabase/Neon/RDS)  │
└──────────────┘     └──────────────────────┘               └──────────────────────┘

💡 Cost Tip: When developing or testing, use the 1-click destroy action in GitHub Actions to tear down all resources when you finish, spending less than $0.20 total per test.

1. Secure Multi-Stage Dockerfile (Fast & SOC2 Compliant) 

# Stage 1: Build Wheels & Compile Dependencies
FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder
WORKDIR /build

ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    gcc build-essential && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --upgrade pip \
    && pip wheel --no-cache-dir --no-deps --wheel-dir /build/wheels -r requirements.txt

# Stage 2: Minimal Non-Root Runtime Container
FROM python:3.11-slim AS runner
WORKDIR /app

ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PORT=8000

# Security: Run as non-root user (UID 10001) for SOC2 compliance
RUN groupadd -g 10001 appgroup && \
    useradd -u 10001 -g appgroup -s /bin/sh -m appuser

COPY --from=builder /build/wheels /wheels
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --upgrade pip \
    && pip install --no-cache-dir /wheels/* \
    && rm -rf /wheels

COPY . /app
RUN chown -R appuser:appgroup /app
USER appuser

EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

2. Terraform ECS Fargate Service ($0 NAT Gateway Architecture) 

# ECS Fargate Service in Public Subnet (Saves $35+/month on NAT Gateways)
resource "aws_ecs_service" "app" {
  name            = "fastapi-ecs-dev-service"
  cluster         = aws_ecs_cluster.main.id
  task_definition = aws_ecs_task_definition.app.arn
  desired_count   = 1
  launch_type     = "FARGATE"

  deployment_minimum_healthy_percent = 50
  deployment_maximum_percent         = 200

  network_configuration {
    subnets          = var.public_subnet_ids
    security_groups  = [var.ecs_security_group_id]
    assign_public_ip = true # Direct route to Internet Gateway - $0 NAT Gateway needed!
  }

  load_balancer {
    target_group_arn = var.target_group_arn
    container_name   = "fastapi-ecs-api"
    container_port   = 8000
  }
}

title: PostgreSQL high availability with only 2 servers: where the third vote comes from
summary:
Many teams have budget for two database servers, not three. Almost every PostgreSQL high-availability guide, on the other hand, opens with "you need at least three nodes".

Both statements are true at the same time. You can run automatic failover with two database servers, but you cannot run it safely with two votes. This post explains why, and where the third vote can come from.

The question every failover has to answer

When a replica stops hearing from the primary, it cannot tell the difference between two situations:

  1. The primary is down.
  2. The network between the two nodes is down, and the primary is happily serving clients.

If the replica promotes itself in case 2, you have split-brain: two primaries accepting different writes. When the network comes back, those two histories cannot be merged automatically, and somebody loses data.

Consensus systems solve this with a majority rule: an action only happens if more than half of the voters agree. With two voters the majority is two. If they disagree, nobody has a majority and nothing happens. That is safe, but it also means no failover.

How Patroni and etcd use the majority

Patroni manages PostgreSQL on each node and stores cluster state in a distributed configuration store (DCS), most often etcd:

  • The primary holds a leader key in etcd and renews it on every HA loop, every loop_wait seconds (default 10).
  • The key expires after ttl seconds (default 30). Only when it expires can a replica take it and promote itself.
  • If the primary cannot update the leader key, Patroni demotes it. In the documentation's words: "In case the update of the leader lock fails, Postgres is immediately demoted and started as read-only." (Patroni's optional failsafe_mode relaxes this when the primary can still reach every other Patroni member.)

So Patroni itself never decides by local opinion: it delegates the "who is primary" decision to etcd. And etcd is a Raft cluster that needs a majority of its members to accept writes. The etcd FAQ gives the numbers:

etcd members Majority Failures tolerated
1 1 0
2 2 0
3 2 1
4 3 1
5 3 2

Two etcd members tolerate zero failures, exactly like one. If one etcd member is on each database server and one server dies, the survivor has 1 of 2 votes, etcd loses quorum, no leader key can be written, and the surviving node cannot become (or even stay) primary. The etcd FAQ also notes that adding a member to reach an even number "doesn't buy additional fault tolerance", which is why the usual recommendation is 3 or 5 members.

The constraint is on voters, not on PostgreSQL instances. That is the door to two-server designs.

Option 1: a third database server

Three nodes, each running PostgreSQL, Patroni and etcd. It is the simplest topology to reason about, and you get a second replica for reads or for synchronous replication. It is also the most expensive option, because the third machine needs the same disk and memory as the others.

Option 2: a witness that only runs etcd

A small VM that runs only etcd, no PostgreSQL and no Patroni. etcd is light, so a modest machine is enough. What matters is placement: the witness must not share a failure domain with either database server (different hypervisor host at a minimum, a different room or site if you have one).

A minimal sketch of the three-member etcd cluster (names and IPs are examples):

# On the witness (repeat on db1 and db2 with their own --name and IPs)
etcd --name witness \
  --initial-advertise-peer-urls http://10.0.0.13:2380 \
  --listen-peer-urls http://10.0.0.13:2380 \
  --listen-client-urls http://10.0.0.13:2379,http://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --advertise-client-urls http://10.0.0.13:2379 \
  --initial-cluster db1=http://10.0.0.11:2380,db2=http://10.0.0.12:2380,witness=http://10.0.0.13:2380 \
  --initial-cluster-state new

And in each patroni.yml, point Patroni at all three:

etcd3:
  hosts: 10.0.0.11:2379,10.0.0.12:2379,10.0.0.13:2379

Use TLS for peer and client traffic in production; it is left out here for brevity.

Now if db1 dies, db2 and the witness still form a majority (2 of 3), the leader key expires, and db2 can take it. If the link between db1 and db2 breaks but both can reach the witness, etcd still has one consistent view and only one node holds the key.

Option 3: let the load balancers vote

Applications rarely connect to PostgreSQL directly. In the common Patroni setup they go through HAProxy, which polls each node's Patroni REST API: GET /primary returns HTTP 200 "only when the Patroni node is running as the primary with leader lock", and HAProxy sends writes to whichever node answers 200.

That makes the load balancers useful observers. They see the cluster from the application side. If most of them cannot reach the primary, the problem is not just the link between the two database nodes; clients are affected too. A design that counts load balancer opinions as votes can supply the third vote with machines you probably already run. This is not something Patroni does out of the box: you need a component that collects those observations, requires a strict majority, and then acts through Patroni (for example via its REST API) without ever bypassing etcd's view of who holds the leader key.

Things to get right with two database nodes

  • Synchronous vs asynchronous replication. With a single replica in strict synchronous mode, losing the replica stops writes on the primary. event_model_payload.headline: PostgreSQL high availability with only 2 servers: where the third vote comes from
event_model_payload.summary:
Many teams have budget for two database servers, not three. Almost every PostgreSQL high-availability guide, on the other hand, opens with "you need at least three nodes".

Both statements are true at the same time. You can run automatic failover with two database servers, but you cannot run it safely with two votes. This post explains why, and where the third vote can come from.

The question every failover has to answer

When a replica stops hearing from the primary, it cannot tell the difference between two situations:

  1. The primary is down.
  2. The network between the two nodes is down, and the primary is happily serving clients.

If the replica promotes itself in case 2, you have split-brain: two primaries accepting different writes. When the network comes back, those two histories cannot be merged automatically, and somebody loses data.

Consensus systems solve this with a majority rule: an action only happens if more than half of the voters agree. With two voters the majority is two. If they disagree, nobody has a majority and nothing happens. That is safe, but it also means no failover.

How Patroni and etcd use the majority

Patroni manages PostgreSQL on each node and stores cluster state in a distributed configuration store (DCS), most often etcd:

  • The primary holds a leader key in etcd and renews it on every HA loop, every loop_wait seconds (default 10).
  • The key expires after ttl seconds (default 30). Only when it expires can a replica take it and promote itself.
  • If the primary cannot update the leader key, Patroni demotes it. In the documentation's words: "In case the update of the leader lock fails, Postgres is immediately demoted and started as read-only." (Patroni's optional failsafe_mode relaxes this when the primary can still reach every other Patroni member.)

So Patroni itself never decides by local opinion: it delegates the "who is primary" decision to etcd. And etcd is a Raft cluster that needs a majority of its members to accept writes. The etcd FAQ gives the numbers:

etcd members Majority Failures tolerated
1 1 0
2 2 0
3 2 1
4 3 1
5 3 2

Two etcd members tolerate zero failures, exactly like one. If one etcd member is on each database server and one server dies, the survivor has 1 of 2 votes, etcd loses quorum, no leader key can be written, and the surviving node cannot become (or even stay) primary. The etcd FAQ also notes that adding a member to reach an even number "doesn't buy additional fault tolerance", which is why the usual recommendation is 3 or 5 members.

The constraint is on voters, not on PostgreSQL instances. That is the door to two-server designs.

Option 1: a third database server

Three nodes, each running PostgreSQL, Patroni and etcd. It is the simplest topology to reason about, and you get a second replica for reads or for synchronous replication. It is also the most expensive option, because the third machine needs the same disk and memory as the others.

Option 2: a witness that only runs etcd

A small VM that runs only etcd, no PostgreSQL and no Patroni. etcd is light, so a modest machine is enough. What matters is placement: the witness must not share a failure domain with either database server (different hypervisor host at a minimum, a different room or site if you have one).

# On the witness (repeat on db1 and db2 with their own --name and IPs)
etcd --name witness \
  --initial-advertise-peer-urls http://10.0.0.13:2380 \
  --listen-peer-urls http://10.0.0.13:2380 \
  --listen-client-urls http://10.0.0.13:2379,http://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --advertise-client-urls http://10.0.0.13:2379 \
  --initial-cluster db1=http://10.0.0.11:2380,db2=http://10.0.0.12:2380,witness=http://10.0.0.13:2380 \
  --initial-cluster-state new

And in each patroni.yml, point Patroni at all three:

etcd3:
  hosts: 10.0.0.11:2379,10.0.0.12:2379,10.0.0.13:2379

Use TLS for peer and client traffic in production; it is left out here for brevity.

Now if db1 dies, db2 and the witness still form a majority (2 of 3), the leader key expires, and db2 can take it. If the link between db1 and db2 breaks but both can reach the witness, etcd still has one consistent view and only one node holds the key.

Option 3: let the load balancers vote

Applications rarely connect to PostgreSQL directly. In the common Patroni setup they go through HAProxy, which polls each node's Patroni REST API: GET /primary returns HTTP 200 "only when the Patroni node is running as the primary with leader lock", and HAProxy sends writes to whichever node answers 200.

That makes the load balancers useful observers. They see the cluster from the application side. If most of them cannot reach the primary, the problem is not just the link between the two database nodes; clients are affected too. A design that counts load balancer opinions as votes can supply the third vote with machines you probably already run. This is not something Patroni does out of the box: you need a component that collects those observations, requires a strict majority, and then acts through Patroni (for example via its REST API) without ever bypassing etcd's view of who holds the leader key.

  • Fencing. After a failover, the old primary must not receive writes again until it has rejoined as a replica.
  • Test it. Kill the primary, freeze it with SIGSTOP, cut the network between the nodes, and measure how long writes stop. A failover you have never tested is an assumption.

Summary

  • Two database servers are fine. Two voters are not.
  • etcd needs 3 (or 5) members for fault tolerance; the third one does not have to run PostgreSQL.
  • Your options for the third vote: a third DB node, an etcd-only witness, or a voting scheme built on the load balancers' view.

title: BT ve Yazılım Ekipleri İçin ISO 27001 Denetiminde Nesnel Kanıt Toplama Rehberi (ISO 19011)
summary:
Yazılım geliştiriciler ve sistem mühendisleri için ISO 27001 denetimleri çoğu zaman sıkıcı bir bürokrasi veya geliştirme hızını kesen bir "evrak işi" gibi algılanır.

Ancak ISO/IEC 27001 standardının 2022 revizyonu ile birlikte denetim dünyası kökten değişti. Denetçiler artık internetten indirilmiş statik PDF politikalarıyla ilgilenmiyor; doğrudan GitHub PR loglarını, Terraform konfigürasyonlarını, CI/CD hatlarını ve AWS CloudTrail kayıtlarını görmek istiyor.

Bu rehberde, uluslararası ISO 19011 (Yönetim Sistemleri Denetim Rehberi) ilkelerine göre bir denetçinin sahada ne aradığını, "nesnel kanıt" (objective evidence) kavramını ve teknik ekiplerin denetime nasıl hazırlanması gerektiğini inceliyoruz.

1. ISO 19011 Kuralı: "Nesnel Kanıt" Nedir?

ISO 19011 Madde 3.8 uyarınca nesnel kanıt: Gözlem, ölçme, test veya doğrulanabilir kayıtlarla varlığı kanıtlanan veridir.

Bir denetçi için:

  • ❌ "Biz zaten kod incelemesi yapıyoruz, herkes dikkat eder." bir kanıt değildir.
  • ✅ GitHub branch protection kuralının açık olduğunu gösteren ekran görüntüsü, son 30 günde ana dala (main branch) atılan PR'lardaki zorunlu onay logları ve squash-merge kayıtları nesnel kanıttır.

2. Dört Temel BT Alanında Denetçi Ne Sorar & Ne İster?

A. Kaynak Kod Güvenliği ve Branch Koruması (Ek-A 8.28)

  • Denetçinin Sorusu: "Geliştiriciler doğrudan production/main dalına kod push edebiliyor mu? Kod inceleme (PR review) zorunlu mu?"
  • Beklenen Kanıt:
    • Repodaki Branch Protection kuralları (en az 1 bağımsız reviewer onayı şartı).
    • Son 3 aya ait 5 rastgele PR incelemesi: Kim açtı, kim onayladı, onaylayan kişi yazarın kendisi mi?
    • Kod havuzunda gizli anahtar (secret) taramasının (gitleaks, trufflehog vb.) pre-commit veya CI kancasında çalıştığına dair loglar.

B. CI/CD Hattı ve Zafiyet Yönetimi (Ek-A 8.8)

  • Denetçinin Sorusu: "Kullandığınız açık kaynak kütüphanelerin (dependency) güvenlik açıklarını nasıl takip ediyorsunuz?"
  • Beklenen Kanıt:
    • CI/CD hattına entegre edilmiş SCA/SAST araçları (Dependabot, Snyk, Trivy).
    • Tespit edilen kritik açıklıkların Jira/ServiceNow biletleri ve SLA takibi (örneğin Kritik açıklar için 7 gün kuralı).

C. Altyapı ve Konfigürasyon Yönetimi (Ek-A 8.9)

  • Denetçinin Sorusu: "Bulut kaynakları ve sunucular elle mi açılıyor, standart hardening şablonu var mı?"
  • Beklenen Kanıt:
    • Altyapının Kod Olarak Yönetimi (IaC - Terraform / OpenTofu).
    • tfsec veya checkov ile altyapı kodunun derleme aşamasında taranması (örneğin 0.0.0.0/0 port açılmasının otomatik engellenmesi).
    • Konfigürasyon sapmalarının (drift) izlenmesi.

D. Erişim Yetkileri ve Ayrılan Personel (Ek-A 5.15 & 5.18)

  • Denetçinin Sorusu: "Şirketten ayrılan bir yazılımcının AWS, GitHub ve VPN erişimleri ne kadar sürede kapatılıyor?"
  • Beklenen Kanıt:
    • İK işten çıkış tarihi ile Active Directory / SSO hesap kapatma logunun zaman damgası (timestamp) karşılaştırması.
    • Production veritabanlarına doğrudan erişim yerine geçici, denetlenen ve yetkilendirilen (bastion / teleport / IAM role) mekanizma kayıtları.

3. Denetim Sırasında Hayat Kurtaran 3 Altın Kural

  1. Yalnızca Sorulan Soruya Cevap Verin: Denetçinin sormadığı sistemleri veya geliştirme aşamasındaki deneysel projeleri gereksiz yere anlatmayın.
  2. Spekülasyon Yapmayın: Bilmediğiniz bir teknik ayrıntı sorulduğunda "Şu an tam logu hatırlamıyorum, sistem kayıtlarına bakıp 10 dakika içinde sunalım" demek, tahmini yanlış bilgi vermekten bin kat daha profesyoneldir.
  3. Sahte / Tarihsiz Kanıt Üretmeyin: Denetim sabahı alelacele oluşturulan Excel listeleri veya geriye dönük sahte toplantı tutanakları kıdemli bir denetçi tarafından anında fark edilir ve doğrudan Majör Uygunsuzluk bulgusuna yol açar.

🛠️ Açık Kaynak Denetçi ve Vaka Çalışma Kiti

ISO 27001 denetimlerinde karşılaşılan gerçek senaryoları ve uygunsuzluk (NCR) yazım kurallarını incelemek isterseniz, GitHub üzerinde yayımladığımız açık kaynaklı kiti inceleyebilirsiniz:

Sistemlerinizi yalnızca denetime hazırlamakla kalmayıp; ISO 19011 ve ISO/IEC 17021-1 uyarınca 3. taraf bağımsız belgelendirme denetimlerini yönetecek uluslararası baş denetçi yetkinliği kazanmak isterseniz:

title: What Really Happens When You Run curl google.com on Linux?
summary:
A step-by-step breakdown of shell parsing, ELF linking, glibc resolver queries, non-blocking TCP handshakes, socket buffers, and the infamous 301 redirect.

You type curl google.com in your terminal and hit enter. Within forty milliseconds, a short snippet of HTML lands on your screen:

 http-equiv="content-type" content="text/html;charset=utf-8">
</span>301 Moved<span class="nt">

301 Moved

The document has moved
 HREF="http://www.google.com/">here.

Most engineers glance at that output and assume curl made a quick HTTP call and printed the response.

That explanation skips almost everything interesting.

Between the moment your finger depresses the enter key and the moment your prompt returns, your machine moves through dozens of discrete subsystems. Bash parses raw keystrokes from a pseudo-terminal. The kernel loads an ELF binary and resolves dynamic libraries through memory maps. The GNU C library queries the Name Service Switch to find out how your machine translates hostnames. A non-blocking TCP socket initiates a three-way handshake across network queues and physical network interfaces.

Then Google rejects your request, sends back a redirect, and curl tears down the socket before you can blink.

Here is the entire mechanical chain, traced down through the system calls, kernel structures, and network packets.

1. The Terminal, the Shell, and the Execve Boundary

Everything begins before curl even exists in memory.

When you type on your keyboard, your terminal emulator (like Alacritty, GNOME Terminal, or Windows Terminal over SSH) sends scan codes across a pseudo-terminal pair (/dev/pts/X). The shell process (usually Bash) sits blocked inside a read() system call on file descriptor 0.

# You can see bash waiting for your input:
read(0, "c", 1)                         = 1
read(0, "u", 1)                         = 1
read(0, "r", 1)                         = 1
read(0, "l", 1)                         = 1
read(0, " ", 1)                         = 1
read(0, "g", 1)                         = 1
...
read(0, "\n", 1)                        = 1

Once the newline byte \n arrives, Bash wakes up. It reads the string into its internal line buffer and begins tokenization.

First, Bash checks for aliases. If you aliased curl to curl -i or curl -s in your .bashrc, Bash substitutes the command string immediately. Next, it looks for shell functions, built-ins, and reserved keywords. None match.

Bash now knows it needs to execute an external binary. To find where that binary lives on disk, it checks its internal command hash table. If you have run curl recently, Bash remembers the exact path /usr/bin/curl. If not, it iterates through the colon-separated directories in your $PATH environment variable:

stat("/usr/local/sbin/curl", ...) = -1 ENOENT (No such file or directory)
stat("/usr/local/bin/curl", ...)  = -1 ENOENT (No such file or directory)
stat("/usr/sbin/curl", ...)       = -1 ENOENT (No such file or directory)
stat("/usr/bin/curl", {st_mode=S_IFREG|0755, st_size=281808, ...}) = 0

Bash finds the executable at /usr/bin/curl.

Now comes the process fork. Bash cannot replace its own running image because it must survive to draw the next prompt. It calls clone() (or fork() on older kernels) with flags like SIGCHLD to spawn an identical child process.

The child process inherits file descriptors 0 (stdin), 1 (stdout), and 2 (stderr), all pointing back to your pseudo-terminal slave. Immediately after cloning, the child calls execve():

execve("/usr/bin/curl", ["curl", "google.com"], [/* 48 vars */]) = 0

The shell image in the child process is instantly overwritten. Bash in the parent process calls wait4() and puts itself to sleep, waiting for the child to finish.

2. The ELF Loader and Dynamic Shared Libraries

The Linux kernel takes control of the new process. It opens /usr/bin/curl and inspects the first four bytes of the file. They must match the standard ELF magic number: 0x7f 0x45 0x4c 0x46 (\x7fELF).

Because curl is compiled as a dynamically linked binary, the kernel does not jump directly into curl's main() function. Instead, it reads the PT_INTERP program header from the ELF file. This header points to the dynamic linker:

/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2

The kernel sets up the process stack with arguments (argv), environment variables (envp), and auxiliary vectors (which provide details like hardware capabilities and random seeds for ASLR). Then it maps the dynamic linker into memory and transfers control to it.

The dynamic linker inspects the DT_NEEDED tags in curl's ELF binary to find every shared library curl relies on. On a typical modern Linux distribution, curl depends on several heavy shared objects:

ldd /usr/bin/curl

The output reveals the dependency graph:

  • libcurl.so.4 (the core transfer engine)
  • libssl.so.3 and libcrypto.so.3 (OpenSSL cryptographic routines)
  • libz.so.1 (compression support)
  • libc.so.6 (standard C runtime)

The dynamic linker maps each of these shared libraries into the process's virtual memory address space using mmap() system calls. It applies relocations, binds symbol addresses, sets memory page protections (marking code pages as read-only and executable), and activates security protections like Full RELRO and stack canaries.

Once dynamic linking finishes, control finally jumps to _start inside curl, which initializes the C runtime and calls main().

3. Argument Parsing and the Easy Handle

Curl starts by parsing its command-line arguments using getopt or internal string parsers.

The argument passed was google.com.

Notice what is missing: there is no URL scheme. You did not specify http:// or https://.

What does curl do? By default, curl inspects the string. It checks if the string starts with a recognized scheme followed by ://. Finding none, curl prepends http:// as the default protocol (though newer versions allow configuring --proto-default).

Because the default protocol is HTTP, curl sets the target destination port to 80.

Curl now allocates its central operational structure: the Curl_easy handle. This structure holds state machines, timeout values, buffer pointers, error buffers, and protocol handlers.

Curl also checks whether its standard output is connected to a terminal by calling isatty(1). If stdout is a terminal, curl configures itself to show transfer progress meters if requested, but hides them for quick responses to prevent cluttering your prompt.

No network packets have moved yet. Everything so far has been local CPU cycles and memory mapping.

4. The Domain Name Resolution (DNS) Pipeline

Curl has a hostname (google.com), but network routers only understand IP addresses. Curl must translate google.com into an IPv4 or IPv6 address.

Curl does not contain hardcoded DNS packet builders. Instead, it relies on the C library by calling the standard POSIX resolver function:

getaddrinfo("google.com", "http", &hints, &res)

This single call triggers an extensive internal investigation inside the Linux operating system.

Step 4A: The Name Service Switch (/etc/nsswitch.conf)

The C library (glibc) opens /etc/nsswitch.conf to check how this specific machine is configured to resolve hosts. It looks for the hosts: line:

hosts: files mdns4_minimal [NOTFOUND=return] dns

This configuration tells glibc the order of operations:

  1. Check local static files first (files).
  2. If not found, attempt multicast DNS (mdns4_minimal).
  3. If not found, query standard DNS servers (dns).

Step 4B: Checking Static Files (/etc/hosts)

glibc opens /etc/hosts and scans it line by line using openat() and read(). It checks if someone mapped google.com to a static IP address like 127.0.0.1.

Unless you are actively intercepting traffic for local development, google.com is not in /etc/hosts. glibc closes the file and moves to the next provider.

Step 4C: Reading the Resolv Configuration (/etc/resolv.conf)

Now glibc needs to know which DNS server to contact. It opens /etc/resolv.conf. On modern systemd-based Linux installations (Ubuntu, Fedora, Debian), you will usually see:

nameserver 127.0.0.53
options edns0 trust-ad

127.0.0.53 is not an external server. It is a local loopback IP address managed by systemd-resolved, a local caching and DNS multiplexing daemon.

Step 4D: The DNS Query on the Wire

glibc creates a UDP socket using socket(AF_INET, SOCK_DGRAM|SOCK_CLOEXEC, 0) and calls connect() to attach the socket to 127.0.0.53:53.

It constructs a DNS query packet asking for two records:

  • An A record (for IPv4)
  • An AAAA record (for IPv6)

It transmits the packet using sendto():

sendto(sockfd, "\x12\x34\x01\x00\x00\x01\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x06google\x03com\x00\x00\x01\x00\x01", 28, 0, ...)

The systemd-resolved service catches this request. If it already has the answer in its local in-memory cache, it replies in less than one millisecond.

If the entry is not cached, systemd-resolved looks at its upstream network interfaces (configured via DHCP or static cloud configurations like AWS Route 53 or Google Cloud DNS at 169.254.169.254 or public DNS like 8.8.8.8). It sends an outbound UDP DNS request across your primary network interface, awaits the upstream answer, caches the result, and writes the response back down to the loopback socket where glibc is waiting in poll().

glibc reads the response using recvfrom(). It parses the DNS answers and hands curl a linked list of addrinfo structures containing resolved IP addresses:

  • IPv4: 142.250.190.46
  • IPv6: 2607:f8b0:4009:81b::200e

Step 4E: The "Happy Eyeballs" Race (RFC 8305)

Modern versions of curl implement Happy Eyeballs.

If both IPv6 and IPv4 addresses are returned, curl does not just pick one and freeze if your local IPv6 routing is broken. It attempts to connect to the IPv6 address first. If the IPv6 connection does not complete within approximately 250 milliseconds, curl simultaneously launches a connection attempt to the IPv4 address. Whichever connection establishes first wins, and curl cancels the slower attempt.

Let us trace the common IPv4 connection to 142.250.190.46:80.

5. Routing, ARP, and Layer 2 Discovery

Curl now has an IP address (142.250.190.46) and a destination port (80). But the Linux kernel cannot just spray packets into thin air. It needs to know which physical interface to use and which local hardware address to target.

The kernel consults its Forwarding Information Base (FIB), commonly known as the routing table:

ip route get 142.250.190.46

The kernel's routing subsystem evaluates the destination IP against its routes:

142.250.190.46 via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0 src 192.168.1.50 uid 1000
    cache

This kernel lookup tells the networking stack three crucial things:

  1. The packet must exit via interface eth0.
  2. The local source IP address to stamp into the IP header is 192.168.1.50.
  3. The destination is not on the local subnet, so the packet must be sent to the default gateway at 192.168.1.1.

Resolving the Gateway MAC via ARP

Ethernet switches do not understand IP addresses. They only route Ethernet frames based on 48-bit MAC addresses.

The kernel checks its internal ARP neighbor cache (ip neigh). It looks for an entry for 192.168.1.1.

If the entry is present (REACHABLE), the kernel grabs the gateway MAC address (for example, 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e).

If the entry has expired or is missing, the kernel pauses transmission and broadcasts an ARP request frame to the entire local broadcast domain:

ARP, Request who-has 192.168.1.1 tell 192.168.1.50, length 28

Your local home router or top-of-rack data center switch hears the broadcast and replies directly with an ARP reply:

ARP, Reply 192.168.1.1 is-at 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e, length 28

The Linux kernel saves this mapping in its ARP table. Now it has everything required to build a physical Ethernet frame.

6. The Non-Blocking TCP Three-Way Handshake

Curl creates the actual communication socket:

int fd = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM|SOCK_NONBLOCK|SOCK_CLOEXEC, IPPROTO_TCP);

Notice the SOCK_NONBLOCK flag. Curl never uses blocking sockets. If a network call blocks, the entire process freezes. By using non-blocking I/O, curl keeps total control over timeouts and event loops.

Curl calls connect():

connect(fd, {sa_family=AF_INET, sin_port=htons(80), sin_addr=inet_addr("142.250.190.46")}, 16) = -1 EINPROGRESS

Because the socket is non-blocking, connect() cannot finish immediately. It returns -1 with an errno of EINPROGRESS. This is completely normal in network programming. It simply means: "The handshake has started in the background; check back in a moment."

Inside the Linux kernel, the TCP engine springs into action.

The SYN Packet

The kernel allocates a socket buffer structure (struct sk_buff, commonly called an skb). It builds the TCP packet:

  • Source port: An ephemeral port chosen randomly from /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_local_port_range (e.g., 48212).
  • Destination port: 80.
  • Sequence number: A cryptographically randomized 32-bit initial sequence number (ISN).
  • Flags: SYN flag set.
  • TCP Options: Maximum Segment Size (MSS), Selective Acknowledgments (SACK Permitted), Window Scale factor, and TCP Timestamps.

The kernel wraps the TCP segment inside an IPv4 packet, sets the TTL to 64, and places it inside an Ethernet frame stamped with the destination MAC of your gateway.

The frame is pushed into the network interface transmission queue (qdisc, like fq_codel). The network driver writes the descriptor to the physical network card's TX ring buffer using Direct Memory Access (DMA). The network card transmits the electrical or optical signal across the wire.

The socket transitions to the SYN_SENT state.

The SYN-ACK Arrival

Across the internet, routers forward the packet to the nearest Google edge POP (Point of Presence). Google's edge load balancer (the Google Front End, or GFE) accepts the SYN and replies with a SYN-ACK packet.

When the electrical signals return to your local network card:

  1. The NIC copies the incoming frame into a host RAM buffer via DMA.
  2. The NIC fires a hardware interrupt (IRQ) to a CPU core.
  3. The kernel interrupt handler schedules a SoftIRQ (software interrupt) via the NAPI (New API) polling subsystem.
  4. The kernel polls the RX ring buffer, wraps the frame in an skb, and feeds it into netif_receive_skb().
  5. The TCP/IP stack strips the Ethernet and IP headers, validates the TCP checksum, matches the packet against your socket's 4-tuple (source IP, source port, dest IP, dest port), and finds the socket waiting in SYN_SENT.
  6. The kernel updates the socket state to ESTABLISHED.
  7. The kernel automatically generates and sends the final ACK packet back to Google, completing the three-way handshake.

Waking Curl

While the kernel was handling packets, curl was waiting inside poll() or ppoll():

ppoll([{fd=3, events=POLLOUT|POLLWRNORM}], 1, {tv_sec=299, tv_nsec=999000000}, NULL, 8) = 1

The moment the socket transitions to ESTABLISHED, the kernel marks the socket descriptor as writable. poll() wakes up. Curl calls getsockopt(fd, SOL_SOCKET, SO_ERROR, ...) to confirm that the connection succeeded without errors.

The TCP tunnel is open.

7. Sending the HTTP Request

Now that the transport layer is established, curl moves to Layer 7 (the application layer).

Curl builds the HTTP request in an internal heap buffer. Because curl defaults to HTTP/1.1 for plain web requests, the buffer contains a simple ASCII string:

GET / HTTP/1.1\r\n
Host: google.com\r\n
User-Agent: curl/8.5.0\r\n
Accept: */*\r\n
\r\n

Notice the components of this request:

  • GET /: The requested path is root.
  • Host: google.com: Mandatory in HTTP/1.1 so multi-tenant reverse proxies know which virtual host you want.
  • User-Agent: curl/8.5.0: Curl identifies itself and its version.
  • Accept: */*: Curl informs the server that it will accept any MIME type in response.
  • An empty line (\r\n\r\n): Signals the end of the HTTP headers.

Curl writes this buffer into the socket using sendto():

sendto(3, "GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: google.com\r\nUser-Agent: curl/8.5.0\r\nAccept: */*\r\n\r\n", 75, 0, NULL, 0) = 75

The sendto() syscall does not send the packet across the internet immediately.

Instead, it copies those 75 bytes from curl's user space memory into the socket's kernel write buffer (sk_write_queue). The kernel packetizes the data, applies TCP segmentation, calculates checksums (often offloaded to the physical NIC via TCP Segmentation Offload, or TSO), and flushes the packet to the transmission ring buffer.

Curl now transitions from writing to reading. It calls poll() again, this time watching for POLLIN (incoming data readable).

8. Google's Edge and the Infamous 301 Redirect

Your request reaches Google's edge infrastructure on port 80.

Google does not serve its search engine over unencrypted HTTP. Serving plain HTTP would expose queries, cookies, and user sessions to eavesdropping and ISP injection.

However, Google cannot simply drop port 80 traffic. If it did, users typing google.com into their browsers would experience connection timeouts. Port 80 exists exclusively to bounce clients over to secure transport.

Google's server software processes your request and crafts an HTTP response:

HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
Location: http://www.google.com/
Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8
Date: Sun, 25 Oct 2026 05:14:22 GMT
Expires: Tue, 24 Nov 2026 05:14:22 GMT
Cache-Control: public, max-age=2592000
Server: gfe
Content-Length: 219

Take a close look at that Location header. It says:

Location: http://www.google.com/

This surprises almost everyone. Why did Google redirect plain http://google.com to http://www.google.com/ instead of jumping straight to https://?

Google maintains strict canonical domain rules. The apex domain google.com first normalizes to the www. subdomain. If you follow that redirect, http://www.google.com/ will issue a second redirect to https://www.google.com/.

Google also appends a tiny fallback HTML payload to the response body:

 http-equiv="content-type" content="text/html;charset=utf-8">
</span>301 Moved<span class="nt">

301 Moved

The document has moved
 HREF="http://www.google.com/">here.

Why include HTML inside a 301 response? For ancient HTTP/1.0 clients or web crawlers that do not automatically follow Location headers, this embedded link allows a human or robot to manually click through to the new address.

9. Receiving the Bytes and Writing to stdout

The packet containing Google's 301 response travels back through your ISP, hits your router, enters your network card, and passes through the kernel's NAPI receive pipeline.

The kernel places the payload into the socket's receive buffer and wakes up curl's waiting poll() call.

Curl calls recv():

recv(3, "HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently\r\nLocation: http://www.google.com/\r\n...", 16384, 0) = 542

Curl reads 542 bytes into its memory buffer.

Curl's HTTP state machine parses the response line: HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently. It parses the headers line by line until it hits the double CRLF (\r\n\r\n).

Here is where standard curl behavior surprises people: curl does not follow redirects by default.

In a web browser, a 301 status code triggers an immediate internal navigation to the URL in the Location header. But curl is a UNIX command-line tool. UNIX tools do not make assumptions about what you want. Unless you explicitly pass the -L or --location flag, curl treats a 301 response as a finished transfer.

By default, curl hides HTTP response headers and only outputs the payload body.

Curl finds the start of the HTML body in its buffer. It prepares to print it. It calls the standard write() system call on file descriptor 1 (stdout):

write(1, "\"co"..., 219) = 219

Because file descriptor 1 points to your pseudo-terminal slave device (/dev/pts/X), the Linux line discipline receives the bytes. The line discipline passes the raw ASCII text across the pseudo-terminal master descriptor to your terminal emulator process.

Your terminal emulator rasterizes the fonts, maps the glyphs against its font cache, submits render draw calls to your graphics server (via Wayland or X11), and the HTML snippet appears on your monitor.

10. Connection Teardown and Process Destruction

The transfer is complete. Curl begins its shutdown routine.

First, it closes the network connection:

close(3) = 0

Inside the kernel, closing the socket file descriptor decrements its reference count to zero. The kernel initiates a clean TCP four-way handshake. It sends a FIN packet to Google's server. Google replies with an ACK, sends its own FIN, and your kernel replies with a final ACK.

Your local TCP socket enters the TIME_WAIT state.

Why TIME_WAIT? The kernel keeps the socket parameters alive for twice the Maximum Segment Lifetime (2 * MSL, typically 60 seconds on Linux) to ensure any delayed or retransmitted packets wandering through the internet do not accidentally collide with a newly opened socket using the same port.

Next, curl frees its memory structures. It deallocates the Curl_easy handle, unloads its protocol state machines, and calls exit_group(0):

exit_group(0)

The kernel reclaims the process's page tables, unmaps the shared libraries, and frees virtual memory pages. The process descriptor enters the EXIT_ZOMBIE state.

The Linux kernel delivers a SIGCHLD signal to the parent process: Bash.

Bash wakes up from its wait4() call:

wait4(28419, [{WIFEXITED(s) && WEXITSTATUS(s) == 0}], 0, NULL) = 28419

Bash collects curl's exit status (0, indicating success). The kernel cleans up the remaining zombie process entry from the process table.

Bash issues another read() call to wait for your next command, prints its prompt string (PS1), and sits waiting for your next keystroke.

The entire sequence took less than fifty milliseconds.

The Practical Diagnostic Arsenal: Tracing It Yourself

You do not have to take any of this on faith. You can observe every single layer of this process on any Linux server using three standard diagnostic tools.

1. Tracing the System Calls (strace)

To see the exact boundary where curl interacts with the Linux kernel, run curl through strace:

strace -f -e trace=process,network,openat,read,write curl -s google.com > /dev/null

You will see the exact sequence: execve, dynamic library mapping, opening /etc/resolv.conf, creating the UDP socket for DNS, the non-blocking connect() returning EINPROGRESS, poll() waiting for readiness, and the final write() to file descriptor 1.

2. Measuring Internal Phase Latency with Curl

Curl contains a built-in formatting engine that extracts microsecond-level timing for every internal phase. Save this snippet in your shell:

curl -w "\
DNS Lookup Time   : %{time_namelookup}s\n\
TCP Connect Time  : %{time_connect}s\n\
App Connect (TLS) : %{time_appconnect}s\n\
Pre-Transfer Time : %{time_pretransfer}s\n\
Start Transfer    : %{time_starttransfer}s\n\
Total Time        : %{time_total}s\n\
HTTP Status Code  : %{http_code}\n\
Redirect URL      : %{redirect_url}\n" \
-o /dev/null -s google.com

Running this command against google.com displays the exact latency profile of your request:

DNS Lookup Time   : 0.004120s
TCP Connect Time  : 0.018450s
App Connect (TLS) : 0.000000s
Pre-Transfer Time : 0.018510s
Start Transfer    : 0.034210s
Total Time        : 0.034320s
HTTP Status Code  : 301
Redirect URL      : http://www.google.com/

Notice that time_appconnect is exactly 0.000000s. Because the request was plain HTTP, zero TLS handshakes occurred.

3. Watching the Wire with tcpdump

Open a second terminal window and run tcpdump on your active interface:

sudo tcpdump -i any -nn "port 80 or port 53"

Then run curl google.com in your primary window. You will see the raw UDP packets heading to port 53 for DNS, followed by the TCP SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK handshake on port 80, the HTTP GET push, the 301 response, and the FIN teardown.

Exactly What Happens When You Pass -L

If you want the real Google search homepage, you must instruct curl to follow redirects using the -L (or --location) flag:

curl -L google.com

When you pass -L, the internal process repeats twice more:

First, curl reads the Location: http://www.google.com/ header. It tears down the first TCP connection, resolves www.google.com, connects on port 80, and issues another GET.

Google's server on www.google.com:80 responds with a second redirect:

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: https://www.google.com/

Curl catches the 302, notes the change in protocol scheme from http:// to https://, changes the target port to 443, resolves the address again, opens a brand new TCP connection, negotiates an OpenSSL TLS 1.3 handshake (exchanging ClientHello, ServerHello, cryptographic certificates, and session keys), and finally issues an encrypted HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1 GET / request.

Only then does Google stream back the full, multi-kilobyte JavaScript and HTML payload of its actual search page.

An Interesting Fact About Curl

Curl was not created as a general-purpose web debugging tool. In 1996, Swedish developer Daniel Stenberg was maintaining an IRC bot called Fraggel. He wanted the bot to automatically fetch currency exchange rates from web pages once a day so IRC users could convert Swedish Kronor to US Dollars in chat rooms.

Finding no lightweight CLI tool that fit his needs, he adopted an open-source utility called httpget, patched it, added FTP support, and renamed it urlget. On March 20, 1998, after adding upload support, he officially released it under the name cURL (Client URL).

Today, Daniel Stenberg still actively maintains the project, and libcurl runs on an estimated twenty billion devices worldwide, including Mars rovers, smart televisions, cars, gaming consoles, and virtually every server running in the cloud.

Summary: The Complete Execution Path

When you strip away the abstraction, a single curl google.com command traverses ten clear boundaries:

  1. Terminal: Readline captures keystrokes over /dev/pts/X.
  2. Shell: Bash expands aliases, locates /usr/bin/curl via $PATH, forks, and calls execve().
  3. Linker: ld.so maps libcurl, libssl, and libc, activating ASLR and page protections.
  4. Initialization: Curl parses arguments, defaults to HTTP port 80, and allocates struct Curl_easy.
  5. Resolver: glibc checks /etc/nsswitch.conf, skips /etc/hosts, and sends UDP queries to 127.0.0.53.
  6. Network Layer: The kernel checks the FIB routing table, finds the default gateway, and resolves the gateway MAC via ARP.
  7. Transport Layer: A non-blocking TCP socket sends a SYN packet, handles SYN-ACK via SoftIRQ, and reaches ESTABLISHED.
  8. Application Layer: Curl formats a plaintext HTTP/1.1 GET request and writes it to the socket buffer.
  9. Edge Response: Google Front End rejects plain HTTP and returns a 219-byte 301 Moved Permanently payload.
  10. Terminal Output: Curl reads the payload, writes it to stdout (fd 1), closes the socket to enter TIME_WAIT, and exits to let Bash draw the next prompt.

Knowing these layers turns mystical network failures into predictable troubleshooting steps. If curl hangs on a server, you no longer guess. You test DNS with dig, check TCP routing with ip route get, inspect socket states with ss -t, and trace syscall bottlenecks with strace.
