A step-by-step breakdown of shell parsing, ELF linking, glibc resolver queries, non-blocking TCP handshakes, socket buffers, and the infamous 301 redirect.

You type curl google.com in your terminal and hit enter. Within forty milliseconds, a short snippet of HTML lands on your screen:

 http-equiv="content-type" content="text/html;charset=utf-8">
</span>301 Moved<span class="nt">

301 Moved

The document has moved
 HREF="http://www.google.com/">here.

Most engineers glance at that output and assume curl made a quick HTTP call and printed the response.

That explanation skips almost everything interesting.

Between the moment your finger depresses the enter key and the moment your prompt returns, your machine moves through dozens of discrete subsystems. Bash parses raw keystrokes from a pseudo-terminal. The kernel loads an ELF binary and resolves dynamic libraries through memory maps. The GNU C library queries the Name Service Switch to find out how your machine translates hostnames. A non-blocking TCP socket initiates a three-way handshake across network queues and physical network interfaces.

Then Google rejects your request, sends back a redirect, and curl tears down the socket before you can blink.

Here is the entire mechanical chain, traced down through the system calls, kernel structures, and network packets.

1. The Terminal, the Shell, and the Execve Boundary

Everything begins before curl even exists in memory.

When you type on your keyboard, your terminal emulator (like Alacritty, GNOME Terminal, or Windows Terminal over SSH) sends scan codes across a pseudo-terminal pair (/dev/pts/X). The shell process (usually Bash) sits blocked inside a read() system call on file descriptor 0.

# You can see bash waiting for your input:
read(0, "c", 1)                         = 1
read(0, "u", 1)                         = 1
read(0, "r", 1)                         = 1
read(0, "l", 1)                         = 1
read(0, " ", 1)                         = 1
read(0, "g", 1)                         = 1
...
read(0, "\n", 1)                        = 1

Once the newline byte \n arrives, Bash wakes up. It reads the string into its internal line buffer and begins tokenization.

First, Bash checks for aliases. If you aliased curl to curl -i or curl -s in your .bashrc, Bash substitutes the command string immediately. Next, it looks for shell functions, built-ins, and reserved keywords. None match.

Bash now knows it needs to execute an external binary. To find where that binary lives on disk, it checks its internal command hash table. If you have run curl recently, Bash remembers the exact path /usr/bin/curl. If not, it iterates through the colon-separated directories in your $PATH environment variable:

stat("/usr/local/sbin/curl", ...) = -1 ENOENT (No such file or directory)
stat("/usr/local/bin/curl", ...)  = -1 ENOENT (No such file or directory)
stat("/usr/sbin/curl", ...)       = -1 ENOENT (No such file or directory)
stat("/usr/bin/curl", {st_mode=S_IFREG|0755, st_size=281808, ...}) = 0

Bash finds the executable at /usr/bin/curl.

Now comes the process fork. Bash cannot replace its own running image because it must survive to draw the next prompt. It calls clone() (or fork() on older kernels) with flags like SIGCHLD to spawn an identical child process.

The child process inherits file descriptors 0 (stdin), 1 (stdout), and 2 (stderr), all pointing back to your pseudo-terminal slave. Immediately after cloning, the child calls execve():

execve("/usr/bin/curl", ["curl", "google.com"], [/* 48 vars */]) = 0

The shell image in the child process is instantly overwritten. Bash in the parent process calls wait4() and puts itself to sleep, waiting for the child to finish.

2. The ELF Loader and Dynamic Shared Libraries

The Linux kernel takes control of the new process. It opens /usr/bin/curl and inspects the first four bytes of the file. They must match the standard ELF magic number: 0x7f 0x45 0x4c 0x46 (\x7fELF).

Because curl is compiled as a dynamically linked binary, the kernel does not jump directly into curl's main() function. Instead, it reads the PT_INTERP program header from the ELF file. This header points to the dynamic linker:

/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2

The kernel sets up the process stack with arguments (argv), environment variables (envp), and auxiliary vectors (which provide details like hardware capabilities and random seeds for ASLR). Then it maps the dynamic linker into memory and transfers control to it.

The dynamic linker inspects the DT_NEEDED tags in curl's ELF binary to find every shared library curl relies on. On a typical modern Linux distribution, curl depends on several heavy shared objects:

ldd /usr/bin/curl

The output reveals the dependency graph:

  • libcurl.so.4 (the core transfer engine)
  • libssl.so.3 and libcrypto.so.3 (OpenSSL cryptographic routines)
  • libz.so.1 (compression support)
  • libc.so.6 (standard C runtime)

The dynamic linker maps each of these shared libraries into the process's virtual memory address space using mmap() system calls. It applies relocations, binds symbol addresses, sets memory page protections (marking code pages as read-only and executable), and activates security protections like Full RELRO and stack canaries.

Once dynamic linking finishes, control finally jumps to _start inside curl, which initializes the C runtime and calls main().

3. Argument Parsing and the Easy Handle

Curl starts by parsing its command-line arguments using getopt or internal string parsers.

The argument passed was google.com.

Notice what is missing: there is no URL scheme. You did not specify http:// or https://.

What does curl do? By default, curl inspects the string. It checks if the string starts with a recognized scheme followed by ://. Finding none, curl prepends http:// as the default protocol (though newer versions allow configuring --proto-default).

Because the default protocol is HTTP, curl sets the target destination port to 80.

Curl now allocates its central operational structure: the Curl_easy handle. This structure holds state machines, timeout values, buffer pointers, error buffers, and protocol handlers.

Curl also checks whether its standard output is connected to a terminal by calling isatty(1). If stdout is a terminal, curl configures itself to show transfer progress meters if requested, but hides them for quick responses to prevent cluttering your prompt.

No network packets have moved yet. Everything so far has been local CPU cycles and memory mapping.

4. The Domain Name Resolution (DNS) Pipeline

Curl has a hostname (google.com), but network routers only understand IP addresses. Curl must translate google.com into an IPv4 or IPv6 address.

Curl does not contain hardcoded DNS packet builders. Instead, it relies on the C library by calling the standard POSIX resolver function:

getaddrinfo("google.com", "http", &hints, &res)

This single call triggers an extensive internal investigation inside the Linux operating system.

Step 4A: The Name Service Switch (/etc/nsswitch.conf)

The C library (glibc) opens /etc/nsswitch.conf to check how this specific machine is configured to resolve hosts. It looks for the hosts: line:

hosts: files mdns4_minimal [NOTFOUND=return] dns

This configuration tells glibc the order of operations:

  1. Check local static files first (files).
  2. If not found, attempt multicast DNS (mdns4_minimal).
  3. If not found, query standard DNS servers (dns).

Step 4B: Checking Static Files (/etc/hosts)

glibc opens /etc/hosts and scans it line by line using openat() and read(). It checks if someone mapped google.com to a static IP address like 127.0.0.1.

Unless you are actively intercepting traffic for local development, google.com is not in /etc/hosts. glibc closes the file and moves to the next provider.

Step 4C: Reading the Resolv Configuration (/etc/resolv.conf)

Now glibc needs to know which DNS server to contact. It opens /etc/resolv.conf. On modern systemd-based Linux installations (Ubuntu, Fedora, Debian), you will usually see:

nameserver 127.0.0.53
options edns0 trust-ad

127.0.0.53 is not an external server. It is a local loopback IP address managed by systemd-resolved, a local caching and DNS multiplexing daemon.

Step 4D: The DNS Query on the Wire

glibc creates a UDP socket using socket(AF_INET, SOCK_DGRAM|SOCK_CLOEXEC, 0) and calls connect() to attach the socket to 127.0.0.53:53.

It constructs a DNS query packet asking for two records:

  • An A record (for IPv4)
  • An AAAA record (for IPv6)

It transmits the packet using sendto():

sendto(sockfd, "\x12\x34\x01\x00\x00\x01\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x06google\x03com\x00\x00\x01\x00\x01", 28, 0, ...)

The systemd-resolved service catches this request. If it already has the answer in its local in-memory cache, it replies in less than one millisecond.

If the entry is not cached, systemd-resolved looks at its upstream network interfaces (configured via DHCP or static cloud configurations like AWS Route 53 or Google Cloud DNS at 169.254.169.254 or public DNS like 8.8.8.8). It sends an outbound UDP DNS request across your primary network interface, awaits the upstream answer, caches the result, and writes the response back down to the loopback socket where glibc is waiting in poll().

glibc reads the response using recvfrom(). It parses the DNS answers and hands curl a linked list of addrinfo structures containing resolved IP addresses:

  • IPv4: 142.250.190.46
  • IPv6: 2607:f8b0:4009:81b::200e

Step 4E: The "Happy Eyeballs" Race (RFC 8305)

Modern versions of curl implement Happy Eyeballs.

If both IPv6 and IPv4 addresses are returned, curl does not just pick one and freeze if your local IPv6 routing is broken. It attempts to connect to the IPv6 address first. If the IPv6 connection does not complete within approximately 250 milliseconds, curl simultaneously launches a connection attempt to the IPv4 address. Whichever connection establishes first wins, and curl cancels the slower attempt.

Let us trace the common IPv4 connection to 142.250.190.46:80.

5. Routing, ARP, and Layer 2 Discovery

Curl now has an IP address (142.250.190.46) and a destination port (80). But the Linux kernel cannot just spray packets into thin air. It needs to know which physical interface to use and which local hardware address to target.

The kernel consults its Forwarding Information Base (FIB), commonly known as the routing table:

ip route get 142.250.190.46

The kernel's routing subsystem evaluates the destination IP against its routes:

142.250.190.46 via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0 src 192.168.1.50 uid 1000
    cache

This kernel lookup tells the networking stack three crucial things:

  1. The packet must exit via interface eth0.
  2. The local source IP address to stamp into the IP header is 192.168.1.50.
  3. The destination is not on the local subnet, so the packet must be sent to the default gateway at 192.168.1.1.

Resolving the Gateway MAC via ARP

Ethernet switches do not understand IP addresses. They only route Ethernet frames based on 48-bit MAC addresses.

The kernel checks its internal ARP neighbor cache (ip neigh). It looks for an entry for 192.168.1.1.

If the entry is present (REACHABLE), the kernel grabs the gateway MAC address (for example, 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e).

If the entry has expired or is missing, the kernel pauses transmission and broadcasts an ARP request frame to the entire local broadcast domain:

ARP, Request who-has 192.168.1.1 tell 192.168.1.50, length 28

Your local home router or top-of-rack data center switch hears the broadcast and replies directly with an ARP reply:

ARP, Reply 192.168.1.1 is-at 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e, length 28

The Linux kernel saves this mapping in its ARP table. Now it has everything required to build a physical Ethernet frame.

6. The Non-Blocking TCP Three-Way Handshake

Curl creates the actual communication socket:

int fd = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM|SOCK_NONBLOCK|SOCK_CLOEXEC, IPPROTO_TCP);

Notice the SOCK_NONBLOCK flag. Curl never uses blocking sockets. If a network call blocks, the entire process freezes. By using non-blocking I/O, curl keeps total control over timeouts and event loops.

Curl calls connect():

connect(fd, {sa_family=AF_INET, sin_port=htons(80), sin_addr=inet_addr("142.250.190.46")}, 16) = -1 EINPROGRESS

Because the socket is non-blocking, connect() cannot finish immediately. It returns -1 with an errno of EINPROGRESS. This is completely normal in network programming. It simply means: "The handshake has started in the background; check back in a moment."

Inside the Linux kernel, the TCP engine springs into action.

The SYN Packet

The kernel allocates a socket buffer structure (struct sk_buff, commonly called an skb). It builds the TCP packet:

  • Source port: An ephemeral port chosen randomly from /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_local_port_range (e.g., 48212).
  • Destination port: 80.
  • Sequence number: A cryptographically randomized 32-bit initial sequence number (ISN).
  • Flags: SYN flag set.
  • TCP Options: Maximum Segment Size (MSS), Selective Acknowledgments (SACK Permitted), Window Scale factor, and TCP Timestamps.

The kernel wraps the TCP segment inside an IPv4 packet, sets the TTL to 64, and places it inside an Ethernet frame stamped with the destination MAC of your gateway.

The frame is pushed into the network interface transmission queue (qdisc, like fq_codel). The network driver writes the descriptor to the physical network card's TX ring buffer using Direct Memory Access (DMA). The network card transmits the electrical or optical signal across the wire.

The socket transitions to the SYN_SENT state.

The SYN-ACK Arrival

Across the internet, routers forward the packet to the nearest Google edge POP (Point of Presence). Google's edge load balancer (the Google Front End, or GFE) accepts the SYN and replies with a SYN-ACK packet.

When the electrical signals return to your local network card:

  1. The NIC copies the incoming frame into a host RAM buffer via DMA.
  2. The NIC fires a hardware interrupt (IRQ) to a CPU core.
  3. The kernel interrupt handler schedules a SoftIRQ (software interrupt) via the NAPI (New API) polling subsystem.
  4. The kernel polls the RX ring buffer, wraps the frame in an skb, and feeds it into netif_receive_skb().
  5. The TCP/IP stack strips the Ethernet and IP headers, validates the TCP checksum, matches the packet against your socket's 4-tuple (source IP, source port, dest IP, dest port), and finds the socket waiting in SYN_SENT.
  6. The kernel updates the socket state to ESTABLISHED.
  7. The kernel automatically generates and sends the final ACK packet back to Google, completing the three-way handshake.

Waking Curl

While the kernel was handling packets, curl was waiting inside poll() or ppoll():

ppoll([{fd=3, events=POLLOUT|POLLWRNORM}], 1, {tv_sec=299, tv_nsec=999000000}, NULL, 8) = 1

The moment the socket transitions to ESTABLISHED, the kernel marks the socket descriptor as writable. poll() wakes up. Curl calls getsockopt(fd, SOL_SOCKET, SO_ERROR, ...) to confirm that the connection succeeded without errors.

The TCP tunnel is open.

7. Sending the HTTP Request

Now that the transport layer is established, curl moves to Layer 7 (the application layer).

Curl builds the HTTP request in an internal heap buffer. Because curl defaults to HTTP/1.1 for plain web requests, the buffer contains a simple ASCII string:

GET / HTTP/1.1\r\n
Host: google.com\r\n
User-Agent: curl/8.5.0\r\n
Accept: */*\r\n
\r\n

Notice the components of this request:

  • GET /: The requested path is root.
  • Host: google.com: Mandatory in HTTP/1.1 so multi-tenant reverse proxies know which virtual host you want.
  • User-Agent: curl/8.5.0: Curl identifies itself and its version.
  • Accept: */*: Curl informs the server that it will accept any MIME type in response.
  • An empty line (\r\n\r\n): Signals the end of the HTTP headers.

Curl writes this buffer into the socket using sendto():

sendto(3, "GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: google.com\r\nUser-Agent: curl/8.5.0\r\nAccept: */*\r\n\r\n", 75, 0, NULL, 0) = 75

The sendto() syscall does not send the packet across the internet immediately.

Instead, it copies those 75 bytes from curl's user space memory into the socket's kernel write buffer (sk_write_queue). The kernel packetizes the data, applies TCP segmentation, calculates checksums (often offloaded to the physical NIC via TCP Segmentation Offload, or TSO), and flushes the packet to the transmission ring buffer.

Curl now transitions from writing to reading. It calls poll() again, this time watching for POLLIN (incoming data readable).

8. Google's Edge and the Infamous 301 Redirect

Your request reaches Google's edge infrastructure on port 80.

Google does not serve its search engine over unencrypted HTTP. Serving plain HTTP would expose queries, cookies, and user sessions to eavesdropping and ISP injection.

However, Google cannot simply drop port 80 traffic. If it did, users typing google.com into their browsers would experience connection timeouts. Port 80 exists exclusively to bounce clients over to secure transport.

Google's server software processes your request and crafts an HTTP response:

HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
Location: http://www.google.com/
Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8
Date: Sun, 25 Oct 2026 05:14:22 GMT
Expires: Tue, 24 Nov 2026 05:14:22 GMT
Cache-Control: public, max-age=2592000
Server: gfe
Content-Length: 219

Take a close look at that Location header. It says:

Location: http://www.google.com/

This surprises almost everyone. Why did Google redirect plain http://google.com to http://www.google.com/ instead of jumping straight to https://?

Google maintains strict canonical domain rules. The apex domain google.com first normalizes to the www. subdomain. If you follow that redirect, http://www.google.com/ will issue a second redirect to https://www.google.com/.

Google also appends a tiny fallback HTML payload to the response body:

 http-equiv="content-type" content="text/html;charset=utf-8">
</span>301 Moved<span class="nt">

301 Moved

The document has moved
 HREF="http://www.google.com/">here.

Why include HTML inside a 301 response? For ancient HTTP/1.0 clients or web crawlers that do not automatically follow Location headers, this embedded link allows a human or robot to manually click through to the new address.

9. Receiving the Bytes and Writing to stdout

The packet containing Google's 301 response travels back through your ISP, hits your router, enters your network card, and passes through the kernel's NAPI receive pipeline.

The kernel places the payload into the socket's receive buffer and wakes up curl's waiting poll() call.

Curl calls recv():

recv(3, "HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently\r\nLocation: http://www.google.com/\r\n...", 16384, 0) = 542

Curl reads 542 bytes into its memory buffer.

Curl's HTTP state machine parses the response line: HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently. It parses the headers line by line until it hits the double CRLF (\r\n\r\n).

Here is where standard curl behavior surprises people: curl does not follow redirects by default.

In a web browser, a 301 status code triggers an immediate internal navigation to the URL in the Location header. But curl is a UNIX command-line tool. UNIX tools do not make assumptions about what you want. Unless you explicitly pass the -L or --location flag, curl treats a 301 response as a finished transfer.

By default, curl hides HTTP response headers and only outputs the payload body.

Curl finds the start of the HTML body in its buffer. It prepares to print it. It calls the standard write() system call on file descriptor 1 (stdout):

write(1, "\"co"..., 219) = 219

Because file descriptor 1 points to your pseudo-terminal slave device (/dev/pts/X), the Linux line discipline receives the bytes. The line discipline passes the raw ASCII text across the pseudo-terminal master descriptor to your terminal emulator process.

Your terminal emulator rasterizes the fonts, maps the glyphs against its font cache, submits render draw calls to your graphics server (via Wayland or X11), and the HTML snippet appears on your monitor.

10. Connection Teardown and Process Destruction

The transfer is complete. Curl begins its shutdown routine.

First, it closes the network connection:

close(3) = 0

Inside the kernel, closing the socket file descriptor decrements its reference count to zero. The kernel initiates a clean TCP four-way handshake. It sends a FIN packet to Google's server. Google replies with an ACK, sends its own FIN, and your kernel replies with a final ACK.

Your local TCP socket enters the TIME_WAIT state.

Why TIME_WAIT? The kernel keeps the socket parameters alive for twice the Maximum Segment Lifetime (2 * MSL, typically 60 seconds on Linux) to ensure any delayed or retransmitted packets wandering through the internet do not accidentally collide with a newly opened socket using the same port.

Next, curl frees its memory structures. It deallocates the Curl_easy handle, unloads its protocol state machines, and calls exit_group(0):

exit_group(0)

The kernel reclaims the process's page tables, unmaps the shared libraries, and frees virtual memory pages. The process descriptor enters the EXIT_ZOMBIE state.

The Linux kernel delivers a SIGCHLD signal to the parent process: Bash.

Bash wakes up from its wait4() call:

wait4(28419, [{WIFEXITED(s) && WEXITSTATUS(s) == 0}], 0, NULL) = 28419

Bash collects curl's exit status (0, indicating success). The kernel cleans up the remaining zombie process entry from the process table.

Bash issues another read() call to wait for your next command, prints its prompt string (PS1), and sits waiting for your next keystroke.

The entire sequence took less than fifty milliseconds.

The Practical Diagnostic Arsenal: Tracing It Yourself

You do not have to take any of this on faith. You can observe every single layer of this process on any Linux server using three standard diagnostic tools.

1. Tracing the System Calls (strace)

To see the exact boundary where curl interacts with the Linux kernel, run curl through strace:

strace -f -e trace=process,network,openat,read,write curl -s google.com > /dev/null

You will see the exact sequence: execve, dynamic library mapping, opening /etc/resolv.conf, creating the UDP socket for DNS, the non-blocking connect() returning EINPROGRESS, poll() waiting for readiness, and the final write() to file descriptor 1.

2. Measuring Internal Phase Latency with Curl

Curl contains a built-in formatting engine that extracts microsecond-level timing for every internal phase. Save this snippet in your shell:

curl -w "\
DNS Lookup Time   : %{time_namelookup}s\n\
TCP Connect Time  : %{time_connect}s\n\
App Connect (TLS) : %{time_appconnect}s\n\
Pre-Transfer Time : %{time_pretransfer}s\n\
Start Transfer    : %{time_starttransfer}s\n\
Total Time        : %{time_total}s\n\
HTTP Status Code  : %{http_code}\n\
Redirect URL      : %{redirect_url}\n" \
-o /dev/null -s google.com

Running this command against google.com displays the exact latency profile of your request:

DNS Lookup Time   : 0.004120s
TCP Connect Time  : 0.018450s
App Connect (TLS) : 0.000000s
Pre-Transfer Time : 0.018510s
Start Transfer    : 0.034210s
Total Time        : 0.034320s
HTTP Status Code  : 301
Redirect URL      : http://www.google.com/

Notice that time_appconnect is exactly 0.000000s. Because the request was plain HTTP, zero TLS handshakes occurred.

3. Watching the Wire with tcpdump

Open a second terminal window and run tcpdump on your active interface:

sudo tcpdump -i any -nn "port 80 or port 53"

Then run curl google.com in your primary window. You will see the raw UDP packets heading to port 53 for DNS, followed by the TCP SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK handshake on port 80, the HTTP GET push, the 301 response, and the FIN teardown.

Exactly What Happens When You Pass -L

If you want the real Google search homepage, you must instruct curl to follow redirects using the -L (or --location) flag:

curl -L google.com

When you pass -L, the internal process repeats twice more:

First, curl reads the Location: http://www.google.com/ header. It tears down the first TCP connection, resolves www.google.com, connects on port 80, and issues another GET.

Google's server on www.google.com:80 responds with a second redirect:

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: https://www.google.com/

Curl catches the 302, notes the change in protocol scheme from http:// to https://, changes the target port to 443, resolves the address again, opens a brand new TCP connection, negotiates an OpenSSL TLS 1.3 handshake (exchanging ClientHello, ServerHello, cryptographic certificates, and session keys), and finally issues an encrypted HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1 GET / request.

Only then does Google stream back the full, multi-kilobyte JavaScript and HTML payload of its actual search page.

An Interesting Fact About Curl

Curl was not created as a general-purpose web debugging tool. In 1996, Swedish developer Daniel Stenberg was maintaining an IRC bot called Fraggel. He wanted the bot to automatically fetch currency exchange rates from web pages once a day so IRC users could convert Swedish Kronor to US Dollars in chat rooms.

Finding no lightweight CLI tool that fit his needs, he adopted an open-source utility called httpget, patched it, added FTP support, and renamed it urlget. On March 20, 1998, after adding upload support, he officially released it under the name cURL (Client URL).

Today, Daniel Stenberg still actively maintains the project, and libcurl runs on an estimated twenty billion devices worldwide, including Mars rovers, smart televisions, cars, gaming consoles, and virtually every server running in the cloud.

Summary: The Complete Execution Path

When you strip away the abstraction, a single curl google.com command traverses ten clear boundaries:

  1. Terminal: Readline captures keystrokes over /dev/pts/X.
  2. Shell: Bash expands aliases, locates /usr/bin/curl via $PATH, forks, and calls execve().
  3. Linker: ld.so maps libcurl, libssl, and libc, activating ASLR and page protections.
  4. Initialization: Curl parses arguments, defaults to HTTP port 80, and allocates struct Curl_easy.
  5. Resolver: glibc checks /etc/nsswitch.conf, skips /etc/hosts, and sends UDP queries to 127.0.0.53.
  6. Network Layer: The kernel checks the FIB routing table, finds the default gateway, and resolves the gateway MAC via ARP.
  7. Transport Layer: A non-blocking TCP socket sends a SYN packet, handles SYN-ACK via SoftIRQ, and reaches ESTABLISHED.
  8. Application Layer: Curl formats a plaintext HTTP/1.1 GET request and writes it to the socket buffer.
  9. Edge Response: Google Front End rejects plain HTTP and returns a 219-byte 301 Moved Permanently payload.
  10. Terminal Output: Curl reads the payload, writes it to stdout (fd 1), closes the socket to enter TIME_WAIT, and exits to let Bash draw the next prompt.

Knowing these layers turns mystical network failures into predictable troubleshooting steps. If curl hangs on a server, you no longer guess. You test DNS with dig, check TCP routing with ip route get, inspect socket states with ss -t, and trace syscall bottlenecks with strace.

title: AWS Just Launched ECS Gateway: What Changes for DevOps Engineers?
summary:
If you've deployed applications on Amazon ECS, you've probably dealt with the networking setup needed to make a container accessible.

Deploying the container is one part. Exposing it often means configuring:

  • An Application Load Balancer (ALB)
  • Target groups and health checks
  • Listener rules
  • Security groups
  • TLS certificates and DNS

You can manage these with Terraform or CloudFormation, but as the number of services grows, so does the infrastructure configuration you have to maintain.

On October 20, 2026, AWS announced Amazon ECS Gateway, a managed ingress solution for ECS services.

The interesting part isn't that AWS invented a new load balancer.

It's that ECS can now manage much of the load balancer infrastructure for you.

Let's look at what changes and what stays the same.

What Is Amazon ECS Gateway?

Amazon ECS Gateway is an ECS resource that defines shared ingress settings for services.

You associate a gateway with one or more ECS clusters, and individual ECS services opt in using a gateway connector.

ECS then provisions or reuses the underlying resources, including:

  • Application Load Balancers
  • HTTPS listeners
  • Target groups
  • Security groups
  • TLS certificates
  • DNS hostnames

Platform teams configure the gateway; application teams connect their services.

Important: ECS Gateway doesn't replace the Application Load Balancer. It automates provisioning and managing ALB-based ingress.

Also, creating a gateway doesn't immediately create an ALB. ECS provisions the first one when a service connects.

Before vs. After ECS Gateway

Imagine three microservices running on ECS:

  • orders-api
  • products-api
  • payments-api

Before ECS Gateway

You could use a shared ALB with separate target groups and host-based listener rules.

However, you'd still configure and maintain those resources yourself, perhaps through Terraform.

                     Application Load Balancer
                               |
                  +------------+------------+
                  |            |            |
             Target Group  Target Group  Target Group
                  |            |            |
              Orders API   Products API  Payments API

Sharing an ALB across ECS services was already possible.

That isn't the new feature.

With ECS Gateway

A platform engineer defines the gateway configuration once and associates it with ECS clusters.

Services add a gateway connector specifying the named container port to expose.

ECS manages the shared ALB and service-specific routing resources, and each connected service gets a generated HTTPS hostname.

What's new is the infrastructure lifecycle management, not the concept of host-based routing.

How ECS Gateway Works

There are three main steps.

Step 1: Create an ECS Gateway

A platform team creates a gateway and defines settings such as:

  • Public or private ingress
  • VPC subnets
  • Security groups
  • AWS WAF configuration
  • Access logging
  • Maximum ALB capacity

The gateway becomes a centrally managed ingress configuration.

Step 2: Associate the Gateway with ECS Clusters

The gateway is associated with one or more ECS clusters.

This allows different application teams to use the same networking standards.

Step 3: Connect ECS Services

An application team adds a gateway connector to its ECS service.

The connector specifies which named container port should receive traffic.

When the service deploys, ECS checks for compatible gateways, creates a gateway route, and provisions or reuses the required infrastructure.

Request Flow

Here's a simplified architecture:

Client
  |
  | HTTPS :443
  v
Shared Application Load Balancer
  |
  | Host-based listener rule
  v
Service Target Group
  |
  v
ECS Task

Each service gets a unique generated URL following a pattern like:

https://.ecs..on.aws

ECS uses the hostname to route incoming requests to the appropriate target group.

One ALB can serve up to 25 ECS services through ECS Gateway.

When existing ALBs reach capacity, ECS can add another, up to the gateway's configured limit.

Getting Started with ECS Gateway Using AWS CLI

Let's look at a simplified example based on the official AWS documentation.

Note: This example assumes you already have an ECS cluster, an ECS service using awsvpc networking, a suitable VPC, and the necessary IAM permissions. It is not a complete production deployment.

Step 1: Create an ECS Infrastructure IAM Role

ECS needs permission to provision and manage the gateway's ingress resources.

The IAM role must trust ecs.amazonaws.com and have the AWS-managed policy:

AmazonECSInfrastructureRoleForGatewayHostSharedALB

Create the role using the AWS CLI in a Bash-compatible shell:

aws iam create-role \
  --role-name ecsInfrastructureRoleForGateways \
  --assume-role-policy-document '{
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [{
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {"Service": "ecs.amazonaws.com"},
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"
    }]
  }'

Attach the managed policy:

aws iam attach-role-policy \
  --role-name ecsInfrastructureRoleForGateways \
  --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonECSInfrastructureRoleForGatewayHostSharedALB

Your IAM identity must also have the necessary ECS permissions and iam:PassRole permission for this infrastructure role.

Step 2: Create the Gateway

For an AWS account with a suitable default VPC:

aws ecs create-gateway \
  --name shared-ingress \
  --infrastructure-role-arn arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/ecsInfrastructureRoleForGateways \
  --configuration '{"hostSharedAlb": {}}'

Replace 123456789012 with your AWS account ID.

If your ECS service runs in a custom VPC, configure the gateway subnets explicitly.

Otherwise, the gateway's default VPC might not match the ECS service.

Verify the gateway:

aws ecs describe-gateway \
  --gateway shared-ingress

Step 3: Associate the Gateway with Your ECS Cluster 

aws ecs associate-gateway-with-cluster \
  --gateway shared-ingress \
  --cluster my-cluster

Wait until the gateway-cluster association becomes ACTIVE before connecting a service.

Step 4: Connect an ECS Service

Assume our orders-api service:

  • Already exists in my-cluster
  • Uses awsvpc networking
  • Has a named task-definition port called api
  • Responds with HTTP 200 at /health

Connect it using:

aws ecs update-service \
  --cluster my-cluster \
  --service orders-api \
  --gateway-connectors '[
    {
      "portName": "api",
      "filters": {
        "accessTypes": ["PUBLIC"]
      },
      "healthCheck": {
        "healthCheckPath": "/health"
      }
    }
  ]'

The connector matches all compatible public gateways associated with the cluster.

It does not select one by gateway name.

Compatibility also depends on VPC and Availability Zone coverage.

Deployment consideration: Changing gateway health-check configuration later may require replacing a target group. AWS documents restrictions on doing this with the ROLLING deployment strategy. Plan these changes carefully.

Once the deployment succeeds, inspect the gateway connection in the ECS service revision.

Look for an ACTIVE connection and its generated serviceUrl.

For the complete setup and verification procedure, refer to the official AWS connection guide.

Why ECS Gateway Matters for DevOps Engineers

I see three particularly useful improvements.

1. Less Repetitive Infrastructure Configuration

Terraform and CloudFormation already help us automate ALB provisioning.

However, we still have to maintain configurations for:

  • Listener rules
  • Target groups
  • Security groups
  • Certificates
  • Resource relationships

ECS Gateway shifts much of this infrastructure lifecycle management into ECS itself.

This could be particularly useful for teams frequently deploying new microservices.

2. More Consistent Networking and Security

In a traditional setup, different application teams might configure their ingress infrastructure differently.

For example:

  • One service uses restricted security groups.
  • Another exposes unnecessary ports.
  • Another has inconsistent routing configurations.

ECS Gateway lets platform engineers establish common networking standards.

Application teams can then connect their ECS services without independently rebuilding the same ingress setup.

Of course, this doesn't remove the need for IAM controls, network security reviews, or application-level authentication.

3. Potential Cost Savings

Application Load Balancers have ongoing costs.

Running a separate ALB for every small microservice can become expensive.

Since ECS Gateway allows up to 25 services to share one ALB, it could help reduce unnecessary load balancer provisioning.

However, there's an important distinction:

ECS Gateway itself has no additional charge, but the underlying AWS resources are still billed.

You still pay for services such as:

  • Application Load Balancers
  • Applicable CloudWatch usage
  • Data transfer
  • Other underlying infrastructure

Actual savings depend on your existing architecture and traffic patterns.

Important ECS Gateway Limitations

Before adopting it in production, there are several limitations worth understanding.

ECS Task

      "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"
    }]
  }'

title: Claude Code Automation: Publish Gates Blocked 23 Bad Posts in 10 Days
summary:
If Claude Code runs anything that publishes, posts, or deletes for you, don't rely on a prompt that says "be careful." Put a small script between the model and the irreversible step, and make that script read the actual output. In 10 days (2026-09-28 to 2026-10-07) one such gate ran 248 times on my Claude Code-run blog pipeline and blocked 37 of those runs. That stopped 23 different posts before they went live.

None of those numbers come from a model's "done!" message. They come from append-only JSON ledgers that every script writes on every run. Below are the counts, the four failures that forced each rule, and the steps to copy. The longer write-up, with the full tables, is on the original post.

What I measured in 10 days

Claude Code writes and edits the Python scripts, a Windows scheduler runs them, and each script appends one JSON line per run under data/ops/. I counted the ledgers line by line on 2026-10-07.

Measure Value
Gate runs (247 Tistory, 1 dev.to) 248
Passed (exit 0) 206
Blocked (exit 1, defect found) 37
Checker itself broke (exit 2) 5
Distinct posts checked 57
Posts blocked at least once 23
Blocked, later fixed and passed 11

Over a longer window, 49 days with runs, the scheduled jobs logged 1,243 unattended runs across 44 jobs. 997 reported success with output, 207 reported success with zero output, and 39 reported failure.

Why the gate blocked posts

One run can carry two defects, so the reasons add up to 38 across the 37 blocked runs:

  • kw-demand (21): the keyword-demand research file was missing or older than 45 days.
  • fig-embed (6): charts were rendered but never inserted into the post body.
  • rel-date (4): relative dates like "this weekend" that turn false if publishing slips a day.
  • kw-grade (3): the target keyword was below the 200 monthly-search bar.
  • fig-numbers (3): a number in a chart appeared nowhere in the post text.
  • fig-count (1): fewer than 2 charts in the post.

Most blocks are boring. That is the point: they are the cheap, mechanical mistakes a model will make while reporting that everything is fine.

The 4 failures that created the rules

Every gate exists because something went wrong while every check said fine.

1. 132 posts shipped with zero images. The pipeline had published 132 posts with no images in the body, and every verification run passed. The check looked at the social preview image and exempted any post that had one. The fix was a shared gate that counts charts actually embedded in the body, which is where fig-embed and fig-count come from.

2. A post went live, then the job crashed before writing its ledger. The daily job published at 05:01:20 and died at 05:03 with ValueError: I/O operation on closed file. A late import replaced sys.stdout with a new wrapper, the old wrapper was garbage-collected, and it closed the shared buffer. No ledger entry meant the next morning's run would have published the same post again. The fix: use sys.stdout.reconfigure(...) instead, and write the ledger line immediately after each publish rather than at the end of the batch.

3. A --dry run rewrote an input file. A dry run of a social-follow script overwrote its target list with 30 candidates the owner had already rejected. The next scheduled run would have followed them, and dev.to has no unfollow API. The rule: dry means no state changes, not "different output." If a dry path writes even one file, it is not dry.

4. Code pasted through a shell heredoc broke the publisher twice. \n inside an f-string became a real newline, which was a SyntaxError. Worse, \b in a regex became the 0x08 control character, so the image counter always returned 0. That one passed syntax checks and surfaced only as "2 charts inserted, 0 images counted." Now any code containing backslashes goes through the file-edit tool, and a control-character scan runs afterward.

Why gates work where prompts don't

A prompt like "verify your work" asks the model to grade itself. Claude Code is good at writing a checker, but it is not a reliable witness to its own run, because the run's log and the run's result can disagree. Failure 2 is exactly that: the post existed and the record of it didn't.

A gate separates the two. It opens the output (the HTML, the chart files, the ledger) and returns an exit code, and the publisher refuses to continue on a defect. Claude Code then has a concrete, machine-readable reason to fix something. Of the 23 stopped posts, 11 were fixed and re-passed; the other 12 never passed in this window, so they never went out through the publisher with the defect.

Copy this setup

  1. Give every checker three exit codes. 0 is clean, 1 is a defect, 2 means the checker itself is broken (no targets found, file unreadable). Finding zero things to check is exit 2, not a pass.
  2. Append one JSON line per run with timestamp, target, exit code, and defect names. If the line count doesn't grow, the check didn't run.
  3. Make the publish step call the gate and stop on exit 1. Put it inside the publisher, not in a checklist someone has to remember.
  4. Write the ledger the moment the irreversible action happens, not at the end of the batch.
  5. Restrict what a completion report may say. In CLAUDE.md, a report can cite only the checker's name and exit code, what a human actually opened, and what the gate cannot see.
  6. Log every failure as symptom, cause, fix, then turn the fix into a check. My 169 incident entries are where most gate rules came from.

A minimal skeleton with the three exit codes and the ledger line:

import json, sys, time
from pathlib import Path

def check(html_path: Path) -> list[str]:
    html = html_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    defects = []
    if html.count("") < 2:
        defects.append("fig-count")
    return defects

def main(paths: list[str]) -> int:
    targets = [Path(p) for p in paths if Path(p).is_file()]
    if not targets:
        return 2  # nothing to check means the checker is broken
    worst = 0
    with open("gate.jsonl", "a", encoding="utf-8") as ledger:
        for t in targets:
            defects = check(t)
            code = 1 if defects else 0
            worst = max(worst, code)
            ledger.write(json.dumps({
                "ts": time.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S"),
                "target": str(t), "exit": code, "defects": defects,
            }) + "\n")
    return worst

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main(sys.argv[1:]))

The publish step then runs this and aborts when the exit code is not 0.

Limits worth knowing

  • A gate with bad measurement lies with confidence. The first live run of a page checker flagged 320 defects across 80 pages. Every one was an analytics beacon failing because the checker opened pages from file://. When every target fails the same way, suspect the gate first.
  • Gates see surface patterns, not quality. A title-hook detector rated a good title as having zero hooks because its word list was incomplete, and it blocked a publish. Expect false positives and keep an explicit override.
  • "Success with zero output" is ambiguous. 207 runs reported success and produced nothing. Most were legitimate, such as a comment watcher with no new comments, so you must define per job what empty means.
  • This is one operator's setup, a single blog platform over a few weeks. It shows the mechanism works here; it is not a benchmark.

You don't need 44 jobs to start. Wrap the one script that publishes, posts, or deletes with a checker that exits 1 on the defect you fear most, and ask Claude Code to append a JSON line per run. For the full ledger tables and the incident details, read the full post on my-blog.org.

Free tools I keep on my own site: 34 calculators and how-to guides - loans, severance pay, take-home salary, savings vs deposits. New ones go out in one email, no ads.

title: n8n 3.0 Is Docker-Only: What Self-Hosters Need to Change Before Upgrading
summary:
If you self-host n8n, version 3.0 is the upgrade you cannot put off planning for. It changes how you install it, how long your Code nodes can run, which nodes still exist, and how one popular credential works. None of it is hard to handle, but every one of these changes can break a workflow that is running fine today.
Here is what is changing, and the checklist I would run through before touching the upgrade button. The release window is October 2026.
Docker becomes the only supported install
Self-hosted n8n becomes Docker-only in 3.0. npm and npx installs stop being supported. If you installed n8n with npm or npx and have been upgrading that way, that path ends here.
The move is to migrate your instance to Docker before you upgrade. That means exporting your workflows and credentials, standing up the Docker container, and confirming everything imports and runs before you point your real traffic at it. Do the migration on a copy first if you can, and keep the old instance running until the Docker one has handled a full day of real workflows without errors.
The Code node timeout drops from 5 minutes to 1 minute
The Code node timeout goes from 5 minutes down to 1 minute. Any Code node that runs longer than 60 seconds will fail after the upgrade.
This is the change most likely to catch people out, because a slow node can sit quietly in a workflow for months. Search your workflows for Code nodes that call slow APIs, process large files, or loop over big datasets. If a node is close to the limit, split the work, move the heavy part to an external service, or cache the result so the node does not have to do it every run.
Three nodes are removed
The Function, Cron, and Interval nodes are removed in 3.0. If any workflow still uses them, it will not run after the upgrade.
Function nodes are replaced by the Code node, which most people already use. Cron and Interval nodes are replaced by the Schedule Trigger node. The fix is a search and replace job: list every workflow that uses one of these nodes, rebuild the logic with the replacement, and test the workflow end to end before upgrading.
AI Agent v1 modes are retired
The AI Agent v1 modes are retired in favor of the Tools Agent. If you built agents on the v1 modes, they need to move to the Tools Agent before the upgrade.
Check each agent workflow, rebuild it on the Tools Agent, and compare the outputs. Agent behavior can shift when the underlying mode changes, so do not assume the new version will answer exactly like the old one. Test with real prompts from your own work, not just a hello world example.
The Slack credential now needs a signing secret
The Slack API credential now requires a signing secret. Workflows that post to Slack or listen for Slack events will fail if the credential is not updated.
Add the signing secret from your Slack app settings to the credential in n8n, then trigger one of the affected workflows and confirm the Slack message actually arrives. This is a five minute fix that is easy to forget and annoying to debug in production.
The prep checklist, in order
List every workflow that uses Function, Cron, or Interval nodes, and rebuild those with the Code node or Schedule Trigger.
Find Code nodes that run longer than 60 seconds and split or move the heavy work.
Move AI Agent v1 workflows to the Tools Agent and test them with real prompts.
Add the Slack signing secret to your Slack API credential and test a Slack workflow.
Migrate your npm or npx install to Docker, and run the Docker instance alongside the old one until it has handled a full day of real workflows.
Back up your workflows and credentials before the upgrade, so you can roll back if something unexpected breaks.
The theme across all of these is the same: 3.0 rewards the people who prepare and punishes the people who click upgrade on a Friday afternoon. The changes are all manageable, but they are breaking changes, which means the old way stops working rather than warning you first.
For the full breakdown with the complete prep checklist and the details on each change, the guide is here: N8n 3.0 Breaking Changes: How to Prepare

title: GNU tar Exit Status 1 on a Folder That Is Still Being Written: Zero-Padded Clips, set -e, and || true
summary:
A nightly tar of a folder of camera clips can finish, write an archive, and still hand back a clip whose tail is nothing but zero bytes. GNU tar does tell you. It tells you with exit status 1, and exit status 1 is the one most backup scripts handle badly: set -e treats it as a crash, and || true treats it as nothing.

This post is about that middle status, what produces it when the folder is still being written to, and how to keep the files that are still open out of the archive in the first place.

Disclosure: I make an Android camera app. Nothing below uses its code or describes how it stores files. Every result comes from the scripts shown, run once on this version:

tar (GNU tar) 1.34

The three exit statuses

The GNU tar manual lists three outcomes: "Successful termination", "Some files differ", and "Fatal error". For an archive being created, the middle one means "some files were changed while being archived and so the resulting archive does not contain the exact copy of the file set". In the runs below, a missing input gave status 2 and a file changing under tar gave status 1.

That middle status is not an error and not a success. It means the archive exists and something in it may not be what you think. A script that collapses it into either of the other two is wrong some of the time.

How the tests fake a recorder

Getting tar to read a file at the exact moment another process writes to it is a race, and races make bad demos. GNU tar has a checkpoint hook, --checkpoint=N --checkpoint-action=exec=..., which runs a command every N records while tar works. I used it to append to, truncate, or delete a clip part way through the run. It stands in for a recorder that has not closed its file yet. It is not a recorder, and real timing will differ.

The setup makes three clips of 3000000 bytes and backdates them by 20 minutes:

#!/bin/bash
# Three finished clips, sizes fixed so every run prints the same numbers.
rm -rf /tmp/tar_demo && mkdir -p /tmp/tar_demo/clips /tmp/tar_demo/backup
cd /tmp/tar_demo
for n in 1 2 3; do head -c 3000000 /dev/urandom > clips/clip$n.mp4; done
touch -d '20 minutes ago' clips/*.mp4
ls clips

Test one: a clip that grows during the run

The nightly job runs under set -e, so any non-zero status stops it. After tar, the script would upload the archive and prune old ones.

#!/bin/bash
# The nightly job, run with set -e. The checkpoint hook stands in for a
# recorder that is still appending to clip3.mp4 while tar reads it.
set -e
cd /tmp/tar_demo
tar czf backup/clips.tgz \
  --checkpoint=50 \
  --checkpoint-action=exec='sh -c "head -c 1000 /dev/urandom >> clips/clip3.mp4"' \
  clips
echo "upload and prune would run here"

Run it and compare clip3 in the archive with clip3 on disk:

#!/bin/bash
HERE=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)
cd /tmp/tar_demo
bash "$HERE/t1_changed.sh"; echo "job exit status: $?"
echo "--- clip3 in the archive vs on disk (bytes)"
tar tvzf backup/clips.tgz clips/clip3.mp4 | awk '{print "archive:", $3}'
stat -c 'disk:    %s' clips/clip3.mp4

Output:

tar: clips/clip3.mp4: file changed as we read it
job exit status: 1
--- clip3 in the archive vs on disk (bytes)
archive: 3005000
disk:    3017000

The upload line did not print. set -e stopped the job at status 1, so tonight's archive was written and then not sent anywhere, and the old archives were not pruned. If the job's alerting checks whether an upload happened, this looks the same as a dead disk.

The archive also holds a shorter clip3 than the disk does. tar recorded the size when it reached the file and read that many bytes. Anything appended after that is simply not in tonight's archive. For a clip that is still recording, that is expected. The point is that status 1 is the one signal that it happened.

Test two: a clip that shrinks during the run

The worse case is a file that gets shorter while tar is reading it. Here the hook truncates live.mp4 to 1000000 bytes once, at checkpoint 100, after tar has started on it.

#!/bin/bash
# Truncate live.mp4 once, at checkpoint 100, while tar is part way through it.
cd /tmp/tar_demo
head -c 3000000 /dev/urandom > clips/live.mp4
tar cf backup/live.tar --checkpoint=1 \
  --checkpoint-action=exec='sh -c "[ \$TAR_CHECKPOINT = 100 ] && truncate -s 1000000 clips/live.mp4; true"' \
  clips/live.mp4
echo "exit status: $?"
rm -rf restore && mkdir restore && tar xf backup/live.tar -C restore
stat -c 'restored size: %s' restore/clips/live.mp4
printf 'non-zero bytes in the last 1000000: '
tail -c 1000000 restore/clips/live.mp4 | tr -d '\0' | wc -c
rm clips/live.mp4

Output:

tar: clips/live.mp4: File shrank by 1976512 bytes; padding with zeros
exit status: 1
restored size: 3000000
non-zero bytes in the last 1000000: 0

tar had already promised the archive a 3000000-byte file in the header, so it kept that promise by padding with zeros. The restored file is the original size. Its last 1000000 bytes contain no non-zero byte at all. A media player may open it and stop early, or may not open it. Either way, the restore looks complete by size, and only the status and a line on standard error say otherwise.

This is also status 1, the same as test one. The status does not tell you which of the two happened. Only the message does.

Test three: a clip deleted during the run

A prune job or a recorder that rotates files can remove a clip after tar has listed the folder and before it opens the file. The status depends on how the file got onto tar's command line.

#!/bin/bash
cd /tmp/tar_demo
reset() { for n in 1 2 3; do head -c 3000000 /dev/urandom > clips/clip$n.mp4; done; }
reset
echo "--- folder named, clip3 deleted mid-run"
tar czf backup/r1.tgz --checkpoint=50 --checkpoint-action=exec='rm -f clips/clip3.mp4' clips
echo "exit status: $?"
reset
echo "--- same files fed as a list on standard input"
printf 'clips/clip1.mp4\0clips/clip2.mp4\0clips/clip3.mp4\0' |
  tar czf backup/r3.tgz --null -T - --checkpoint=50 --checkpoint-action=exec='rm -f clips/clip3.mp4'
echo "exit status: $?"
reset
echo "--- same files named one by one"
tar czf backup/r2.tgz --checkpoint=50 --checkpoint-action=exec='rm -f clips/clip3.mp4' \
  clips/clip1.mp4 clips/clip2.mp4 clips/clip3.mp4
echo "exit status: $?"
reset

Output:

--- folder named, clip3 deleted mid-run
tar: clips/clip3.mp4: File removed before we read it
tar: clips: file changed as we read it
exit status: 1
--- same files fed as a list on standard input
tar: clips/clip3.mp4: Cannot stat: No such file or directory
tar: Exiting with failure status due to previous errors
exit status: 2
--- same files named one by one
tar: clips/clip3.mp4: Cannot stat: No such file or directory
tar: Exiting with failure status due to previous errors
exit status: 2

Name the folder and a vanished file is status 1, with the folder itself reported as changed. Feed the files as a list, which is what a find pipeline does, or name them one by one, and the same deletion is status 2 with Exiting with failure status. Two scripts that archive the same clips can disagree about whether the same night was a failure.

Test four: turning the warning off

The usual next step is to silence the message. On this version:

#!/bin/bash
cd /tmp/tar_demo
HOOK='sh -c "head -c 1000 /dev/urandom >> clips/clip3.mp4"'
echo "--- --warning=no-file-changed"
tar czf backup/w1.tgz --warning=no-file-changed --checkpoint=50 --checkpoint-action=exec="$HOOK" clips
echo "exit status: $?"
echo "--- --ignore-failed-read --warning=no-file-changed"
tar czf backup/w2.tgz --ignore-failed-read --warning=no-file-changed --checkpoint=50 --checkpoint-action=exec="$HOOK" clips
echo "exit status: $?"

Output:

--- --warning=no-file-changed
exit status: 1
--- --ignore-failed-read --warning=no-file-changed
exit status: 1

Both runs printed nothing and both returned status 1. The first switch removed the one line that said which file changed, and the status stayed. The second switch did not change the status here either.

The manual's warnings page says the file-changed keyword "applies only if used together with the ‘--ignore-failed-read’ option". The tar 1.35 release notes add a fix: "Fix --ignore-failed-read to ignore file-changed read errors as far as exit status is concerned." I tested 1.34, so on 1.35 or later the second run may return 0. I did not check. That is a reason to be careful: on a newer tar, that pair of switches could hide a changed or zero-padded clip completely, status included.

The same warnings page also says warning messages "do not affect the exit code of tar command". On this version, the file-changed case did. I would trust the status you observe on your own tar over either sentence.

Test five: the || true fix

The other common fix is to stop set -e from firing at all. Here the folder name has a typo.

#!/bin/bash
# The common "fix": swallow the status. The folder name is misspelled.
set -e
cd /tmp/tar_demo
tar czf backup/nightly.tgz clipz || true
echo "job carried on"
stat -c 'archive size: %s bytes' backup/nightly.tgz
tar tzf backup/nightly.tgz | wc -l

Output:

tar: clipz: Cannot stat: No such file or directory
tar: Exiting with failure status due to previous errors
job carried on
archive size: 45 bytes
0

|| true hides status 2 as well as status 1. The job carried on with a 45-byte archive holding no files, which would then be uploaded and would count as the newest backup when the pruning step runs.

What I would run instead

Two changes. First, keep files that are still being written out of the archive, so status 1 becomes rare instead of nightly. Second, handle the three statuses as three different things.

#!/bin/bash
# Archive only clips nobody has written to for 10 minutes, then treat
# tar's three outcomes as three different things.
cd /tmp/tar_demo || exit 2
out="backup/clips-$(date +%F).tgz"
find clips -type f -name '*.mp4' -mmin +10 -print0 |
  tar czf "$out" --null -T -
st=${PIPESTATUS[1]}
case $st in
  0) echo "archive complete: $(tar tzf "$out" | wc -l) clips" ;;
  1) echo "WARNING: a clip changed during the run, archive kept, check it" >&2 ;;
  *) echo "FAILED with status $st, archive discarded" >&2; rm -f "$out"; exit "$st" ;;
esac

The -mmin +10 test picks only clips nobody has modified in the last 10 minutes. -print0 with --null -T - hands tar the exact names, spaces and all. The case reads tar's own status from PIPESTATUS, not the status of find. Because the names arrive as a list, a clip deleted after find saw it is a status 2 (test three), and the script throws that archive away rather than keeping a partial one.

The test adds a fresh live.mp4 next to the three settled clips:

#!/bin/bash
HERE=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)
cd /tmp/tar_demo
for n in 1 2 3; do head -c 3000000 /dev/urandom > clips/clip$n.mp4; done
touch -d '20 minutes ago' clips/*.mp4
head -c 3000000 /dev/urandom > clips/live.mp4   # still being written
bash "$HERE/nightly.sh"; echo "exit status: $?"
tar tzf backup/clips-*.tgz

Output:

archive complete: 3 clips
exit status: 0
clips/clip2.mp4
clips/clip3.mp4
clips/clip1.mp4

Three clips archived, live.mp4 skipped, status 0. It goes into tomorrow night's archive, once nothing has written to it for 10 minutes.

Pick the number of minutes from your own recorder. It has to be longer than the longest gap between two writes to an open clip. If the recorder writes rarely, 10 is too short.

Checklist

  • Do not run a nightly tar under bare set -e without handling status 1 yourself.
  • Do not append || true to it. That also swallows status 2.
  • Keep the message. --warning=no-file-changed removes the one line that names the file.
  • Archive files that have stopped changing, chosen by age or by a rename the writer does when it closes the file.
  • Read the message on status 1. file changed and File shrank are different problems with the same status.
  • Restore one archive now and then and play a clip from the end of it, not the start.

Things I did not test

  • tar 1.35 or later. The --ignore-failed-read change is from its release notes, not from a run.
  • A real recorder. The hook appends, truncates or deletes at a checkpoint, which is not how any real writer times its writes.
  • bsdtar, BusyBox tar, or tar on a phone. Their statuses and messages may differ.
  • Compression failures. The manual says a failed compressor makes tar exit with that program's status. I did not trigger one.
  • Network or FUSE-mounted folders. Not tried.

Sources. Quotes are from the GNU tar manual (single-page version and its warnings section) and the tar 1.35 release announcement. Outputs are pasted unedited.

If you want an old phone recording clips in the background so there is a folder like this to back up, the app I make is Background Camera RemoteStream on Google Play. Nothing above depends on it.

Status 1 is tar saying the archive exists but is not the folder. Read it as exactly that.

exit status: 2
--- same files named one by one
tar: clips/clip3.mp4: Cannot stat: No such file or directory
tar: Exiting with failure status due to previous errors
exit status: 2

Name the folder and a vanished file is status 1, with the folder itself reported as changed. Feed the files as a list, which is what a find pipeline does, or name them one by one, and the same deletion is status 2 with Exiting with failure status. Two scripts that archive the same clips can disagree about whether the same night was a failure.

Test four: turning the warning off

The usual next step is to silence the message. On this version:

#!/bin/bash
cd /tmp/tar_demo
HOOK='sh -c "head -c 1000 /dev/urandom >> clips/clip3.mp4"'
echo "--- --warning=no-file-changed"
tar czf backup/w1.tgz --warning=no-file-changed --checkpoint=50 --checkpoint-action=exec="$HOOK" clips
echo "exit status: $?"
echo "--- --ignore-failed-read --warning=no-file-changed"
tar czf backup/w2.tgz --ignore-failed-read --warning=no-file-changed --checkpoint=50 --checkpoint-action=exec="$HOOK" clips
echo "exit status: $?"

Output:

--- --warning=no-file-changed
exit status: 1
--- --ignore-failed-read --warning=no-file-changed
exit status: 1

Both runs printed nothing and both returned status 1. The first switch removed the one line that said which file changed, and the status stayed. The second switch did not change the status here either.

The manual's warnings page says the file-changed keyword "applies only if used together with the ‘--ignore-failed-read’ option". The tar 1.35 release notes add a fix: "Fix --ignore-failed-read to ignore file-changed read errors as far as exit status is concerned." I tested 1.34, so on 1.35 or later the second run may return 0. I did not check. That is a reason to be careful: on a newer tar, that pair of switches could hide a changed or zero-padded clip completely, status included.

The same warnings page also says warning messages "do not affect the exit code of tar command". On this version, the file-changed case did. I would trust the status you observe on your own tar over either sentence.

Test five: the || true fix

The other common fix is to stop set -e from firing at all. Here the folder name has a typo.

#!/bin/bash
# The common "fix": swallow the status. The folder name is misspelled.
set -e
cd /tmp/tar_demo
tar czf backup/nightly.tgz clipz || true
echo "job carried on"
stat -c 'archive size: %s bytes' backup/nightly.tgz
tar tzf backup/nightly.tgz | wc -l

Output:

tar: clipz: Cannot stat: No such file or directory
tar: Exiting with failure status due to previous errors
job carried on
archive size: 45 bytes
0

|| true hides status 2 as well as status 1. The job carried on with a 45-byte archive holding no files, which would then be uploaded and would count as the newest backup when the pruning step runs.

What I would run instead

Two changes. First, keep files that are still being written out of the archive, so status 1 becomes rare instead of nightly. Second, handle the three statuses as three different things.

#!/bin/bash
# Archive only clips nobody has written to for 10 minutes, then treat
# tar's three outcomes as three different things.
cd /tmp/tar_demo || exit 2
out="backup/clips-$(date +%F).tgz"
find clips -type f -name '*.mp4' -mmin +10 -print0 |
  tar czf "$out" --null -T -
st=${PIPESTATUS[1]}
case $st in
  0) echo "archive complete: $(tar tzf "$out" | wc -l) clips" ;;
  1) echo "WARNING: a clip changed during the run, archive kept, check it" >&2 ;;
  *) echo "FAILED with status $st, archive discarded" >&2; rm -f "$out"; exit "$st" ;;
esac

The -mmin +10 test picks only clips nobody has modified in the last 10 minutes. -print0 with --null -T - hands tar the exact names, spaces and all. The case reads tar's own status from PIPESTATUS, not the status of find. Because the names arrive as a list, a clip deleted after find saw it is a status 2 (test three), and the script throws that archive away rather than keeping a partial one.

The test adds a fresh live.mp4 next to the three settled clips:

#!/bin/bash
HERE=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)
cd /tmp/tar_demo
for n in 1 2 3; do head -c 3000000 /dev/urandom > clips/clip$n.mp4; done
touch -d '20 minutes ago' clips/*.mp4
head -c 3000000 /dev/urandom > clips/live.mp4   # still being written
bash "$HERE/nightly.sh"; echo "exit status: $?"
tar tzf backup/clips-*.tgz

Output:

archive complete: 3 clips
exit status: 0
clips/clip2.mp4
clips/clip3.mp4
clips/clip1.mp4

Three clips archived, live.mp4 skipped, status 0. It goes into tomorrow night's archive, once nothing has written to it for 10 minutes.

Pick the number of minutes from your own recorder. It has to be longer than the longest gap between two writes to an open clip. If the recorder writes rarely, 10 is too short.

Checklist

  • Do not run a nightly tar under bare set -e without handling status 1 yourself.
  • Do not append || true to it. That also swallows status 2.
  • Keep the message. --warning=no-file-changed removes the one line that names the file.
  • Archive files that have stopped changing, chosen by age or by a rename the writer does when it closes the file.
  • Read the message on status 1. file changed and File shrank are different problems with the same status.
  • Restore one archive now and then and play a clip from the end of it, not the start.

Things I did not test

  • tar 1.35 or later. The --ignore-failed-read change is from its release notes, not from a run.
  • A real recorder. The hook appends, truncates or deletes at a checkpoint, which is not how any real writer times its writes.
  • bsdtar, BusyBox tar, or tar on a phone. Their statuses and messages may differ.
  • Compression failures. The manual says a failed compressor makes tar exit with that program's status. I did not trigger one.
  • Network or FUSE-mounted folders. Not tried.

Sources. Quotes are from the GNU tar manual (single-page version and its warnings section) and the tar 1.35 release announcement. Outputs are pasted unedited.

If you want an old phone recording clips in the background so there is a folder like this to back up, the app I make is Background Camera RemoteStream on Google Play. Nothing above depends on it.

Status 1 is tar saying the archive exists but is not the folder. Read it as exactly that.

title: The Silent SEO Killer: How I Lost 30% of Organic Traffic on a Site Migration
summary:
We’ve all been there. You migrate a site to a new server or change your permalinks, feeling confident because the new UI looks great. Then, a week later, you open Google Search Console and see a massive cliff: a 30% drop in organic traffic.

A migration is never just about moving files. It’s a complex DNS and routing operation. When it goes wrong, search engines don't forgive easily.

After spending three days debugging a client's botched migration, I realized that 90% of post-migration traffic drops are caused by four easily preventable technical issues. Here is the checklist I now strictly follow before and after any site move.

1. The Silent Fail: Broken Internal Links (404s)

When you change URLs, it's easy to miss internal links in old blog posts or documentation. If a crawler hits a 404 page, it stops traversing that path. Too many 404s, and your site's crawl budget takes a hit.

How to audit: Don't just click around manually. You need to extract all links from a page and check their HTTP response codes.
Instead of writing a complex Python script with requests and BeautifulSoup, I usually run a quick batch scan.

(Example: I use the bulk dead link scanner on Site Tools Box to scan the top 50 pages of the site. It crawls the DOM, sends HEAD requests to every anchor tag, and spits out a list of any 404s or 500s in seconds.)

2. The TTL Trap: DNS Propagation and AAAA Records

You updated the A record to the new server IP, but did you check the AAAA record? If you have an IPv6 record pointing to the old server, users on IPv6 networks (which is a huge percentage of mobile traffic) will still hit the dead server.

How to audit: Use a thorough DNS lookup. You need to verify A, CNAME, MX (don't forget emails!), and TXT records.
Before you switch the nameservers, lower your TTL (Time To Live) to 300 seconds at least 24 hours in advance. This ensures that when you make the switch, global ISPs pick up the change instantly rather than caching the old IP for 48 hours.

3. The Redirect Chain Nightmare

You moved from http://website.com/old-post to https://website.com/new-post.
If your redirects look like http -> https -> www -> new-url, you are burning server resources and leaking PageRank with every hop.

The rule: Every old URL should 301 redirect to its final destination in exactly one hop.

How to audit: Write down your 10 most valuable URLs (highest traffic pages). Check their status codes.
You can use an HTTP header/status checker to see the exact response and how long it takes the server to respond. If it's a 301, ensure Location headers point directly to the final HTTPS URL.

4. The Pre-Migration Domain Vetting

If you are migrating to a brand new domain, buying a clean domain is half the battle. If the previous owner was running a PBN (Private Blog Network) or was penalized by Google, your traffic will never recover.

How to audit: Before you even pay for a domain, do a deep Whois lookup. You need to check the creation date, the registrar, and most importantly, whether the domain has been dropped and re-registered multiple times.
A quick RDAP lookup is usually enough to reveal the registration history. If it was created 3 weeks ago but has 10,000 backlinks, run away.

Summary Checklist

  1. Lower DNS TTL 24 hours prior.
  2. Verify A, AAAA, and CNAME records.
  3. Ensure single-hop 301 redirects for all legacy URLs.
  4. Crawl the entire new site to find dead internal links.
  5. Submit the new sitemap.xml to Google Search Console immediately.

The Takeaway
A successful migration isn't a visual success; it's a routing success. Take 30 minutes to run these technical diagnostics before you hit "deploy" in production. Your organic traffic (and your client) will thank you.
